docs.title: Requirements and first run
docs.text:
The first profile is Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-4: 480×480 ST7701S panel, 240×240 RGB565 LVGL UI, GT911 touch and 2× hardware scaling. You need a MicroPython firmware with LVGL and the display_driver, rgbpanel and gt911 modules already installed. Copying files to generic MicroPython does not install LVGL or its drivers. The IDE does not flash firmware or modify boot.py.

  1. Pick the board in the selector next to Run. Its profile and the 240×240 resolution are applied to the project as one undoable operation; widget positions, sizes and fonts scale to the new resolution, each axis on its own, and widgets that remain out of bounds are reported. The points of a Line widget do not scale.
  2. Press Run (F5): a single serial port is used automatically, otherwise you are asked once. The choice is a local per-board preference and is not saved in the project; Change Port… updates it. C code is available through Project → Export C Code… and cannot be uploaded to a board.
  3. The connection opens by itself and stays open for the console and REPL. Disconnect in the status bar releases the port for other tools.
  4. Device → Connect and Device Information check firmware, LVGL, memory, buffers, touch and compatibility without starting anything. This check imports display_driver and may initialize the display; port enumeration alone does not do it.
  5. Upload Project copies without running; Upload and Run copies and starts. F5 uses the entry chosen in the selector and Shift+F5 stops it.

The Buzzer component uses the pin from the buzzer key of the board profile: GPIO1 on the Waveshare RP2350 and the speaker through audio.py on the ESP32-4848S040. When the profile has no such key, as on the STM32H7, calls do nothing and the IDE reports it. A project whose saved profile predates this key uses the one from the built-in profile with the same id.

The selector choice and the board profile are saved in the project (runTarget, board) and travel with the file; the serial port does not, because it depends on the computer. Use as default for new projects, in the same selector, stores run target, board and resolution in local preferences; Remove default restores the initial behavior.

The application is generated in build/board/<profile-id>/ and installed under /lms_apps/app_<hash>/. The hash comes from the projectId saved in the project, so projects with the same name do not replace each other; Save As creates a new id. Projects created before the id receive one the next time they are saved in the IDE, and their old directory stays on the board. The CLI does not save, so it keeps using the name-based directory for those files. All sources are compiled before reset and transfer; errors are mapped to the original handler and line and do not activate the new version. The probe checks minimum MicroPython/LVGL versions, modules, APIs, resolution and touch against the project profile. Upload uses a staging directory, verifies file sizes and keeps the previous version in .previous. It does not delete unrelated directories or user files. After an interrupted upload, retry: staging is recreated and the active version is not replaced until verification succeeds.

The firmware driver owns the framebuffers, touch and LVGL timer. Generated code does not import lvsim, allocate another framebuffer or create a second event loop. The application remains active through the driver timer after bootstrap finishes.

docs.title: STM32H7_CORE V1.3
docs.text:
The STM32H7_CORE V1.3 (1024×600) profile uses the 1024×600 RGB565 LTDC IPS panel, GT911 touch and 1× scaling. It requires MicroPython 1.29 or later, LVGL 9.5 or later, and the display_driver, gt911 and st_ltdc modules. Pick the board in the selector next to Run; the logical resolution is 1024×600.

The connection uses UART1 through a CH340 adapter at 115200 8N1, normally /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux. Native USB is not used. The IDE sets DTR=1 and RTS=0 before opening the port, waits 3 seconds for boot and keeps the same port open for probing, upload, execution and console. Do not use mpremote or another program on the same port: RTS=1 holds the board in reset and every reopening causes a hard reset. Restart uses a soft reset without reopening the port. Applications are installed under /flash/lms_apps/; autostart only affects /flash/main.py and does not modify display_config.py or other user files.

docs.title: ESP32-4848S040
docs.text: The ESP32-4848S040 (480×480) profile uses native 480×480 RGB565 resolution, GT911 touch and 1× scaling. It requires MicroPython 1.29 or later, LVGL 9.5 or later, and the display_driver and gt911 modules. Panel support is integrated into the display driver: a separate rgbpanel module is not required. The USB serial connection uses mpremote, normally on /dev/ttyUSB0; applications are installed under /lms_apps/ without modifying boot.py or main.py.

docs.title: Live editing
docs.text: While an application started from the IDE is running, Device → Live Editing sends design changes to the board about half a second after the last edit, with no restart. It rebuilds all pages off screen, shows the page open in the designer, and then deletes the old ones. Python module state survives, but widget state such as a typed text or a slider position returns to the design values. Code, Buzzer or Timer changes are not sent: the status bar asks you to press F5.

docs.title: Console, Stop and autostart
docs.text:
The Device Console incrementally shows output and tracebacks produced after bootstrap and accepts REPL commands while the session is ready. The continuous reader pauses during commands that need the port, ensuring a single serial owner. Cancel operation interrupts a blocked command. Stop in the Device menu always targets the board, even when the simulator is selected; F5 and Shift+F5 use the selected destination. Stop removes application modules from the import cache and calls display_driver.stop(). The last image may remain visible because scan-out continues after the timer stops. Every new run performs a soft reset to avoid stale timers and modules.

Install Autostart… is separate from F5. It replaces /main.py with a recognizable launcher and backs up an existing main.py under ~/.config/lvgl-mpy-studio/autostart-backups/<board-id>/<app>/<transaction>/ (or XDG_CONFIG_HOME). Identity uses machine.unique_id(), not the USB port. Every transaction verifies launcher and backup hashes; manual edits, invalid manifests or missing backups block restoration without overwriting files. Remove Autostart… only acts on the current transaction launcher for the selected app.

If an autostart application becomes unresponsive, use the safe/recovery mode provided by the board firmware, or power it down, open another MicroPython tool and remove only the recognizable /main.py launcher. Do not format the filesystem: application files remain under /lms_apps/.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
lvgl-mpy-studio --language en device list
lvgl-mpy-studio --language en device info --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device upload project.json --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device run project.json --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device stop --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device reset --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device repl --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device autostart-install project.json --port /dev/ttyACM0
lvgl-mpy-studio device autostart-remove project.json --port /dev/ttyACM0

Subcommand and option names are always in English. If a project has no embedded profile, add --board-profile <id>. upload and run accept --output <directory>. Projects contain a portable profile copy and can be opened without the corresponding local catalog entry.

Ctrl+C returns status 130 for non-interactive commands. In the interactive REPL it interrupts the remote program; leave the REPL with Ctrl+] as documented by mpremote. The port is released when the command exits. Do not open the IDE, a REPL and another serial monitor on the same port at once.

docs.title: Language and profiles
docs.text: Settings → Language switches Italian/English immediately and saves the preference without changing the project. Device → Manage Board Profiles… provides create, edit, duplicate, delete and restore operations. Changes persist only with Apply. Editing a built-in profile creates a user customization; deleting it hides it. Projects retain their portable copy and are updated only through Update Project Profile, with undo.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text:
A profile can list the Montserrat sizes of its firmware in fonts, for example "fonts": [14, 16, 24, 32, 40]. Text asked in a size the board lacks is drawn in the nearest one, in the designer preview, in the simulator and on the board alike. A profile without the list is taken to have 14, 16 and 24; a project without a board uses the five sizes of the simulator, 14, 16, 24, 32 and 40.

On every upload the IDE reads the fonts the firmware really has. If they differ from the profile, the code is generated for the fonts of the board and a notice says so: add the list to the profile to see the same text in the preview. Device → Device Information shows the list as fonts.

Common errors:

  • device.busy: close REPLs, serial monitors or other IDEs using the port.
  • device.permissions: check the serial port permissions and your distribution's rules; do not copy files as root.
  • device.absent: reconnect the board and select the port again after a reset or USB disconnection.
  • device.timeout: check that the board responds; interrupt any blocked program before retrying.
  • device.prerequisites: install a firmware with the required modules, or fix the profile resolution or touch setting.
  • device.resolution: set the project to the profile's logical size; 240×240 for this Waveshare, not 480×480.
  • device.transfer.incomplete: repeat the upload and check free space and the USB connection.
  • device.autostart.not-owned: /main.py is not a recognizable IDE launcher, so it is not removed.

Raw MicroPython tracebacks are preserved in the console.

docs.title: Case study: EIM-01, an industrial monitor
docs.text:
EIM-01 is the largest application built with LVGL MPY Studio so far: an operator panel that watches a temperature and controls a fan. It is in examples/eim-01, for a 1024×600 display, and in examples/eim-01-480 with a layout of its own for 480×480.

It was built by an AI agent, from a prompt, through the MCP server: the agent created the project, placed the widgets, wrote the code, rendered the pages, played the scenarios and recorded the visual tests with the same tools described in that guide. Nobody drew it by hand in the designer. The checks listed below are the agent's own, and the result has not been reviewed line by line by a person.

What it is not. There is no fan and no sensor: the values come from a simulation inside the application, and it has not been run on a board. It shows what the tool can carry as an application, not a finished device. The last section says what is missing to make it one.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Overview: temperature, humidity, fan speed and power; a temperature chart with the alarm threshold; the fan command, with the requested and the confirmed speed shown apart.
  • Trends: history over 1, 5 and 15 minutes with minimum, maximum and average, and a pause that stops the scrolling while the acquisition goes on.
  • Alarms: a list with the states active, acknowledged and cleared.
  • Diagnostics: link state, age of the data, sequence number, uptime, free memory.
  • Settings: thresholds, refresh rate, data source, and the scenario to simulate.

Five scenarios drive it: normal operation, a temperature that climbs past the threshold, a fan that stalls while its command stays the same, a link that is lost for twelve seconds and comes back, and the recovery to normal values.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
Pages 5 Widgets and timers 256 Handlers 48 General code about 500 lines of MicroPython Generated application for the STM32H7 board 7 files

The interface is made of widgets of the project, the same a person places in the designer, not of objects created by code. The logic is in the general code and in the handlers, apart from the code that creates the screens: ring buffers limited to 900 samples, validation of each value received, the alarm states, the fan ramp.

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
• In the simulator, by the agent, through a list of cases it recorded when it made the example: page changes, the fan ramp from 1500 to 2400 RPM at an 80% command, the alarm above 40 °C and its acknowledgement while the condition lasts, the stalled fan, the lost link and the automatic recovery, a missing value shown as N/A.
  • By visual tests that anyone can repeat. Three scenarios are stored with the project and replayed on a simulated clock, so that every run is the same:
lvgl-mpy-studio test examples/eim-01/project.json

It makes 17 comparisons between pages and scenarios, to the pixel. - By generating the application for the STM32H7_CORE board and, in the 480×480 version, for the ESP32-4848S040.

docs.title: What bringing it to version 0.6 showed
docs.text:
The example was made with version 0.4. Opening it again with 0.6 gave two findings, both left visible:

  • Font sizes the board lacks. Several labels use sizes 11 and 13, which the firmware of the STM32H7 board does not have: they are drawn at 14. Version 0.4 said nothing; 0.6 lists each one as a warning.
  • A reference image with a changing value. The Diagnostics page shows the free memory, which changed with the new generator: one of the 17 comparisons failed until the image was regenerated. A page under visual test should not show such a value.

docs.title: What is missing to make it a device
docs.text:
1. A person's review. The application was written and checked by an agent. It reads well and its tests pass, but its alarm logic and its limits have not been examined by an engineer as a real panel would require.

  2. Hardware. Run it on the STM32H7_CORE board, where it has never been uploaded.

  3. A real temperature and a real fan. The data source can be set to TCP, serial or BLE in the interface, but only the simulation is implemented.
  4. Blocks for the hardware. A temperature sensor on I2C and a fan on PWM are the blocks planned for LVGL MPY Studio and not written yet; this example is their first user.
  5. Settings that survive a restart: today they are kept in RAM only.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Hardware blocks. Two new components under Hardware in the toolbox: Digital Output (a pin on or off: LED, relay) and Digital Input (a pin that is read, with debounce and the events PRESSED, RELEASED and CHANGED). The pin is typed as a number or as a name such as PA5. They work in the simulator, where the output writes its changes in the Output panel and the input is set from code with simulate(). Both were tried on the STM32H7_CORE board, with its two LEDs and its two keys.
  • Blocks from other people. Settings → Manage Blocks… lists the blocks with their origin, author and licence, adds one from a folder, removes it, reloads them and opens the blocks folder; the toolbox follows at once. A project keeps a copy of such blocks, so it opens on a computer that lacks them; a project that uses blocks is saved as version 4, which earlier IDEs refuse instead of misreading. The module a block provides for the simulator runs on the PC, like the code of a project: use blocks from people you trust.
  • Pages for whoever evaluates the project: the stack from the display controller to the agent, how the project was built and by whom, what is verified and how, and a case study. The README is now a front page; its reference material moved to docs/development.md.
  • examples/eim-01: an industrial monitor of 5 pages and 256 widgets with simulated data, built by an AI agent through the MCP server, with a 480×480 version and visual tests.
  • Help → Online Documentation (F1) opens the pages of the project, https://copper-and-code.github.io/lvgl-mpy-studio/; the address is also in the About window. The pages will be published when the repository becomes public.
  • Writing a block. docs/blocks.md builds one step by step, and examples/blocks/blinker is the finished example, ready to install.
  • MCP: list_blocks describes the blocks with their properties, methods and events; project_info says which blocks the project uses.
  • The self-test has a ninth scenario for the blocks, and now fails a step when the IDE raises an error that it would otherwise only print.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The launcher of single-file executables no longer carries the old name: its modules are lms_boot and lms_licenses, its marker is LMSAPP01, and the Windows runtimes describe themselves as LVGL MPY Studio. Games already built keep working, because each carries its own launcher.
  • Blocks, first step (see docs/plugins-plan.md). The Buzzer is no longer written inside the IDE: it is a block, a folder with a description and its MicroPython modules, read by the new core/blocks.py. Nothing changes for projects and for the generated files, which are the same byte for byte. Blocks copied into the blocks folder of the settings are read and checked, but not offered yet.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Self-test. lvgl-mpy-studio selftest uses the IDE as a person would — toolbox, page, Properties panel, code editor, Save As, simulator and touch — and writes a report with PASSED or FAILED for each step, with pictures of what failed. --show shows the IDE at work. Eight scenarios: the full tour, save and open again, pages, resolution, pictures and fonts, Python modules, Timer and Buzzer, and errors.
  • Print Sources. File → Print Sources… (Ctrl+P) prints the source open in the editor or all the sources of the project, with line numbers, the colours of the editor, wrapped long lines, and a header and footer on each page. It has a preview, and a PDF comes from the system print dialog.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Upload progress. Sending an application to a board opens a small window with a bar that follows the bytes sent, the file being written, the time elapsed and an estimate of the time left, and a Cancel button. On boards reached through mpremote the bar moves inside a file by estimate, from the speed of the last upload to that board. It appears when the upload lasts more than a moment. Until now the only sign was a file count in the status bar, which stood still for most of a long upload.
  • Changing the resolution, or the board of the project, fits the page to the window again, as View → Fit to Window does. Each page is fitted when it is shown; other changes keep the zoom.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A widget chosen with a double click in the toolbox was placed twice in a project with several pages: once where you clicked, and again at the first click on another page. Found by the self-test.
  • On Windows, started from LVGL_MPY_STUDIO.exe, a console window flashed four times at almost every operation: the IDE compiles four files with mpy-cross and each run opened its own window. The compiler, the C toolchain and mpremote are now started without a window. It had been so since the first Windows package.
  • On Windows, closing the IDE or ending a command while the RAM measurement or a page preview was running left a simulator process alive for some seconds and printed an error, because its temporary folder could not be removed. Such processes are now stopped first. Found by running the self-test on Windows 11.
  • The warning about fonts and free RAM appeared by mistake from the second upload on: the memory was read while the previous application was still running. It is now read after the reset, with the display driver loaded.
  • When the application did not start after an upload, the warnings found before were lost; they are now shown with the error, in the IDE, on the command line and through MCP.
  • The portable Windows package did not start on Windows: it carried a copy of ICU 72 next to Qt, which hid the icuuc.dll of the system and lacks the functions Qt asks for. The package no longer includes ICU; the package of 0.6.0 starts on a real Windows. Wine did not show the fault, because it starts a program even when imported functions are missing.
  • The Windows packages had no icon: the program file, the taskbar and the windows showed a generic one. The windows have the icon on Linux too.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Images. A picture chosen for an Image widget is converted to PNG, made no larger than the screen and stored inside the project file. It is drawn in the simulator, on boards, in executables, in the browser version and in the C export. MCP tools add_image and remove_image; project_info lists the images. Pictures that cost much memory, and image widgets whose picture is missing, are reported as warnings. Until now a chosen file path was written into the generated code and never drawn, and a project with assets could not be uploaded to a board.
  • Fonts. A TrueType or OpenType file chosen for the font property is stored in the project and converted to LVGL's format for each size in use, by a converter written for the IDE on top of Qt: no Node.js or other tool is needed. Compared with LVGL's built-in Montserrat, made by the official converter from the same file, the metrics are the same and fewer than two pixels in a thousand differ, by one level of sixteen. Kerning is converted too, with the same values wherever the built-in font has it. On upload a warning says when the fonts would take more than half the free RAM of the board. MCP tools add_font and remove_font. The C export includes them too, loaded from memory, which needs LV_USE_FS_MEMFS.
  • From a prompt to an app. examples/weather is a weather station built by an AI agent through the MCP server, with the recorded session of its 24 tool calls; docs/mcp-demo.md describes it and a test replays it.
  • MCP: list_widget_types takes names_only and types and returns the default values; list_boards returns the font sizes of each board.
  • A font size the target lacks and characters outside the built-in font are reported as warnings, by the MCP tools and when generating.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Shorter names on the board and in generated files. Applications are installed under /lms_apps instead of /lvgl_ide_apps; the generated modules are lms_buzzer and lms_probe; the web page loads lms_web.js; the markers in exported C are lms:new-handlers. An autostart installed by 0.4 is still recognised, and C files exported by 0.4 keep working with their markers. Applications already on a board under the old folder are left there: remove the folder by hand. Module names starting with lms_ are reserved.
  • The ESP32-4848S040 and Waveshare RP2350 profiles list the Montserrat sizes read from the real boards: 14, 16, 24, 32 and 40.
  • A new project is named “Untitled”.
  • MCP answers are compact JSON instead of indented: an agent reads about half the characters.
  • The product is now LVGL MPY Studio. The command is lvgl-mpy-studio (lvgl-ide still works), the Python package is lvgl_mpy_studio, and the packages are named LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-…. Settings and the ~/.config/lvgl-ide folder of earlier versions are copied on first start.
  • English is the language of the code: interface texts, comments, messages, examples and documents. The Italian interface is unchanged and the Italian documents remain next to the new English manual and web publishing guide.
  • Three English interface texts changed: the F5 action is Start, the toolbar is Run toolbar and a custom board profile is Custom profile.
  • The examples are examples/<game>/project.json, with English names and comments; tris is now tictactoe.
  • The IDE, the command line and the MCP server start in English. Italian is still available under Settings → Language and with --language it.
  • Deleting a container deletes the widgets inside it. Copy, cut and duplicate take them too, and they keep their place inside the copy.
  • lvgl-mpy-studio build writes to dist/ next to the project, as the IDE does, when --output is not given.
  • App packages no longer contain project.json.
  • A handler set on a page without an event is SCREEN_LOADED. An event the object does not have is refused.
  • The MCP tool remove_widget returns the names of everything it removed.
  • The IDE package is 4.7 MB smaller: it ships only the names the code editor completes instead of the whole binding API.
  • The Simulator panel no longer has an unused path for running the C build.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Choosing a picture that is still above 512 kB once converted to PNG raised an error inside the undo step instead of showing a message.
  • The free space of an STM32H7 board was reported as zero: it was read from the root instead of the filesystem apps are written to.
  • Text in sizes 32 and 40 was drawn at 24 in the simulator and on boards, although the runtime has those fonts. The sizes now come from the target: a board profile can list them in fonts, the upload reads them from the board, and a project without a board uses the five sizes of the simulator. The STM32H7_CORE profile lists the five its firmware has.
  • The order of the widget declarations in the exported ui.c changed from one export to the next.
  • Deleting a container left its children on the page at the wrong position.
  • Widgets inside a container were checked against the screen with coordinates relative to the container, so outOfBounds and the "outside the screen" notice were wrong for them.
  • The simulator always started from the first page, while boards started from the initial page of the project.
  • simulate and visual scenarios could not read a widget the project code never names (ui.<name> raised AttributeError).
  • About eighty error messages reached agents and the command line in Italian whatever the language.
  • An unexpected error could end the MCP server.
  • After an unexpected error during an upload, every later upload answered device.session.busy.
  • A traceback of the app on the board containing words such as "resource" or "not found" was reported as a busy or missing serial port.
  • A board profile without minimum firmware versions raised an error when the board answered.
  • A broken custom board profile file stopped the IDE from starting.
  • A simulated wait could block for a very long time when the app stopped answering.
  • Uploads over UART are about 4.5 times faster: measured on the STM32H7 board, 100 kB take 22 s.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Python modules. A project can hold its own .py modules, which handlers, the general code and other modules import by name (import utils).
  • The project tree has a Python Modules node. Its context menu offers New, Open, Rename and Delete, and a double click opens a module.
  • Modules are edited in the existing code editor, with undo and redo, highlighting, completion and syntax checks.
  • Module names cannot be paths, MicroPython modules, files the IDE generates or handler names.
  • A module created in the editor starts with import lvgl as lv and import ui, and a hint explains why they are needed.
  • What do you want to do? lists each module like a component: import it, call its public functions, classes and upper-case constants. The open module shows its own functions.
  • Modules in every pipeline. Modules are included in the simulator, the upload to boards (as bytecode, with precompilation) and the MicroPython export for a board. They are also included in Debug and Release folder builds, in the single-file executables for Linux and Windows, and in the browser version.
  • The generated folder has a manifest.json with the ordered list of modules. Every build takes its modules from it, and stops with a clear error if it is missing or inconsistent.
  • A module that was removed or renamed is deleted from the generated folder, together with its bytecode.
  • The C export warns that Python modules are not part of it.
  • MCP tools for modules. The new tools are list_modules, create_module, rename_module and delete_module; get_code and patch_code take module as an alternative to handler. project_info lists the modules. Existing tools keep their arguments and answers.
  • Project revisions.
  • project_info, get_code and list_modules return a SHA-256 revision of the project file.
  • Every MCP tool that writes the project accepts expected_revision and returns the revision it wrote. A file changed in the meantime is reported as a structured revision_conflict error, and nothing is written.
  • Changes made outside the IDE.
  • Before saving, the IDE checks that the file on disk is still the one it opened or last saved, for example when an MCP agent or the command line wrote it meanwhile. If the file changed, the IDE asks whether to reload it, save a copy, overwrite it or cancel; Cancel is the default. A deleted file can be recreated or saved elsewhere.
  • Save As asks before replacing another file.
  • Single-file executable for Windows. Run → Build Single-File Executable… now works on Windows too. The --for windows and --for linux options build for the other system. A Linux game built on Windows comes as a .tar.gz, to keep its execute permission.
  • Games in the browser. Run → Open in Browser, lvgl-mpy-studio build --web and lvgl-mpy-studio web build a folder with the page, a WebAssembly runtime of MicroPython and LVGL, and the compiled game, ready for a static host. The folder includes an .htaccess for Apache and LiteSpeed hosts. The runtime is built by runtime/build_web.sh. A publishing guide is available in Italian.
  • Italian user manual, docs/manual.it.md.
  • Project schema 3 for projects with modules. Projects without modules are still written as schema 2, byte for byte.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Errors in modules.
  • A syntax error names the module and its line, and is never reported on the handler that imports the module.
  • In a runtime traceback, the line where the error happened comes first in the Errors panel. The handler that led there is marked "called from here".
  • Double-clicking a row opens the module or handler at that line and highlights it.
  • Confirmations before risky module changes. Renaming or deleting a module that code still imports asks first, with a warning that the old imports will stop with ImportError. Imports are never rewritten.
  • Read-only code while running. While the simulator runs, a bar above the code editor explains why the code is read-only and offers Stop and Edit.
  • Resolution sizes.
  • The resolution menu lists the common sizes 240×240, 480×480, 1024×600 and 1024×1024, even when a board has the same size.
  • Project settings list the common sizes and those of the known boards.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Runtime errors in the simulator did not appear in the Errors panel. The simulator prints tracebacks on standard output, while the IDE read only standard error. This also affected handler errors in 0.3.
  • Custom… in the resolution menu raised an error and did nothing.
  • The Change Port, Manage Board Profiles, Use as Default and Remove Default entries of the destination menu did nothing.
  • Boards whose firmware starts a MicroPython shell that needs a second Ctrl+C, such as some ESP32-4848S040 builds, failed every operation with could not enter raw repl. The IDE now sends repeated Ctrl+C when it connects, and retries once after that error.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Modules.
  • Renaming or deleting a module does not update the code that imports it; the IDE warns and lists those places.
  • Modules created through MCP start empty, without the imports the editor adds.
  • The C export does not include Python modules.
  • Projects with modules (schema 3) cannot be opened by 0.3, which refuses them clearly.
  • External changes.
  • There is no file watcher: the IDE notices a change only when it saves.
  • The revision check is not a lock: a program writing at the very moment of the save can still be overwritten. The same applies to expected_revision over MCP.
  • Simulator. The code is read-only while the simulator runs.
  • Browser version. It has been checked in Chromium only.
  • Documentation. The user manual and the web publishing guide are available in Italian only.

docs.title: Decision log
docs.text:
• New IDE in Python 3.11+ and PySide6 6.12.0 (LGPL), separate from lvgl-mpy-builder.
  • The core (core, gen, build, sim) does not import Qt and is available from the CLI.
  • The TypeScript generator was ported to Python, verified with byte-for-byte golden files at commit 5c217fa1536d4c78b01d07a2dbfcc9055fb59cdc.
  • Native Linux x86-64 target; MicroPython 1.29.0, PyDevices 58d18ce, bindings 7740c2fae0daa10992f5f8fe54acf670a70e2d3b (LVGL 9.5.0).
  • The v2 JSON project keeps the user's Python code; the C target generates stubs and reference comments.
  • A single MicroPython unix runtime supports the IDE, SDL and headless backends through lvsim_io.
  • RGB565 rendering, 800×480 by default; one resolution per project.
  • The C target uses the same lv_conf.h with LV_CPYTHON_BUILD, which selects LV_STDLIB_CLIB; the LVGL cache includes the configuration hash. Unused LVGL drivers and C++ shaders are excluded from the build without changing upstream.
  • The C spinner uses the same animated arc as the MicroPython generator, not lv_spinner_create: this makes rendering identical on the first tick.
  • Headless parity tests use LVSIM_TICK_MS=0; normal behavior keeps the monotonic clock.
  • The MicroPython release profile uses FROZEN_MANIFEST and a build cache based on the hash of the generated sources, with no patch to the unix port.
  • Packaging uses PyInstaller onedir and AppImage; Qt stays in separate shared libraries. The container test needs access to the Docker socket, and the test on a clean Zorin install is manual.
  • Native Windows x86-64 is v1.1 of the IDE and simulator; v1 stays Linux only so it is not slowed down.
  • The Windows toolchain is MinGW-w64 cross-compiled from Linux, without MSVC: same GCC family and no toolchain needed on the development PC.
  • The simulator transport is TCP on 127.0.0.1 with a session token on both systems, avoiding the divergence between Unix sockets and named pipes.
  • User code is stopped with the protocol's STOP message and KeyboardInterrupt, not POSIX signals.
  • The LVGL tick uses the monotonic lvsim.ticks_ms() (CLOCK_MONOTONIC/QueryPerformanceCounter), not the Windows port's system clock.
  • Python platform differences are centralized in lvgl_mpy_studio/platform.py; the core forbids POSIX APIs and writes UTF-8 text with explicit LF newlines.
  • Standalone Windows apps do not open a console: GUI PE subsystem, with stdout and stderr in <project>.log.
  • For the C target on Windows, only existing MSYS2/w64devkit installations are detected; no portable toolchain is included or installed automatically, and a guide is shown if it is missing.
  • The Windows distribution includes both a portable ZIP and a per-user Inno Setup installer in %LOCALAPPDATA%; there is no code signing in v1.1.

docs.title: Reference divergence
docs.text: As of 2026-10-28, the public commit above still declares LVGL 9.3 for MicroPython and does not contain the 30/30 runner cited as a prerequisite. The port's golden files therefore describe that generator, not proven 9.5 compatibility. The v2 path uses the APIs at the pin and requires separate runtime checks.

docs.title: Compact MicroPython generator (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The requirement for output byte-identical to the TypeScript generator is dropped: it verified the port and was not a product requirement. reference/corpus remains as a set of projects to generate; the text comparison is replaced by compiling the result and by behavior and pixel parity tests.
  • ui.py exposes as attributes only the widgets used by user code (ui.name) or that own a handler. If the code uses ui in any form other than ui.something, for example getattr(ui, ...), all of them stay exposed.
  • objects and globals() are gone. Empty handlers generate no code or callback unless code calls them. load_page, load_page_anim, get_current_page and the PAGE_<NAME> constants have stable names and are generated only when used; the old names with the project prefix no longer exist.
  • Groups of identical constant styles on several objects become shared lv_style_t objects, which reduces bytecode and RAM. add_style costs more than a single set_style during creation, but overall startup improves because there is less source to compile. Suspending refresh with enable_style_refresh was tried and rejected: the final recalculation cancels the gain.
  • The C generator does not change.

docs.title: Non-visual components (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• Buzzer and Timer live in lvgl_mpy_studio/core/components.py, outside widgets.json: they are not LVGL objects and the C generator ignores them with a warning.
  • ui.buzzer1 is the lms_buzzer module, generated only when the component is present, so there are no extra classes or objects. ui.timer1 is an lv.timer, created only if it has a handler or code uses it; its handler receives the timer as the e argument.
  • In the simulator the buzzer writes a line ESC LVSIM_TONE frequency milliseconds to stdout, which the IDE intercepts and plays: this avoids changing the native protocol and rebuilding the runtimes. Outside the IDE the module stays silent.
  • The pin is in the optional buzzer key of the board profile (pin or audio). QtMultimedia is loaded only on the first sound.

docs.title: RAM and flash budget (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• Flash is the sum of the files that would go on the board. RAM is measured by running the project in the headless runtime for 15 iterations of the LVGL loop, so it includes objects created by code, and excludes video buffers.
  • The runtime is 64-bit and the boards are 32-bit: RAM is an overestimate, stated in the tooltip and not corrected with unmeasured coefficients.
  • Profiles contain no invented capacities: the comparison uses memoryFree and filesystemFree read at connection and saved in local preferences.

docs.title: Editor help and C target (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• C leaves the selector: it does not run handlers and serves for exporting, so it becomes Project → Export C Code…. The export writes only the four portable files to export_c/ next to the project; main.c and Makefile are tied to the simulator and are needed only to compile. A project saved with a C destination opens on the Simulator; the CLI keeps --target c.
  • Suggestions are a child widget of the editor, not a popup: on Wayland the QCompleter popup is rejected and does not appear.
  • The suggested actions live in lvgl_mpy_studio/core/actions.py, and tests/test_actions.py runs them all on the real runtime, so the IDE cannot suggest calls that do not exist.

docs.title: LVGL preview in the designer (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The canvas shows a frame from the headless runtime (LVSIM_DUMP), about 15 ms per page, on a copy of the project without user code: a broken handler does not affect the designer.
  • WidgetItem objects stay above the frame for selection and dragging. While dragging, the frame is re-rendered with the pending geometry, so the real widget follows the cursor with no duplicate; the project changes only on release. The Toolbox drop preview is always drawn by Qt because it is not in the frame yet. Without a frame the IDE uses Qt drawing.
  • The frame is recomputed only when the visible project changes, not the code. The option is in the View menu and is on by default.

docs.title: Garbage collector in the main thread (2026-11-06)
docs.text: • Budget and preview work in Python threads, and the garbage collector runs in the thread that allocates: a Qt object in a reference cycle could be destroyed outside the main thread, causing rare segfaults in the event loop. lvgl_mpy_studio/ui/gc_guard.py turns off automatic collection and runs it from a main-thread timer.

docs.title: Licenses (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The IDE is GPL-3.0-or-later, copyright Nunzio Raciti. Generated code is MIT, so users' products do not inherit the GPL.
  • The parts that end up in projects or executables are also MIT: lvgl_mpy_studio/gen/output/, native/lvsim/ and runtime/display_driver.py. A dependency with a more restrictive license must not enter these parts. See LICENSING.md.

docs.title: Interface (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The IDE keeps PySide6 with the Fusion style and follows the system color scheme. Icons are Material Design Icons through QtAwesome, as the only runtime addition.
  • theme.icon loads only the mdi6 font and the packages include only that font: the other fonts bundled with QtAwesome have different licenses and are unused.
  • On Wayland the Adwaita decoration plugin draws no border on the sides and bottom, so the window paints one in a 1 px margin. X11 and Windows draw their own.
  • The dock layout has a version: a saved layout from an older version is ignored once.

docs.title: Live editing on the board (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The script re-executes ui.py in the namespace of the running module, rebuilds all pages off screen, loads one, and deletes the old ones. It is general: added, removed and moved widgets need no per-property code, at the cost of resetting widget state. The old page stays visible if the build fails.
  • Only the design is sent. upload_key covers code, Buzzer, Timer, display and board; if it differs from the last upload, the IDE asks for F5, because the board has neither the handlers nor the modules.
  • The LVGL tick runs through micropython.schedule, so it interleaves between bytecodes in the same thread, not during a C call.
  • Measured on the ESP32-4848S040 with a two-widget page: 0.39 s per update, free memory stable over repeated updates.

docs.title: Examples at any resolution (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The games read the real size with lv.display_get_default() when the page loads and place every widget from there, with a unit of 1/240 of the short side. The IDE needs no special mode: picking a board already sets the resolution. The designer still shows the original layout.
  • The size cannot be read at module level: in the simulator app_events is imported before the display exists.
  • The initialization functions clear their lists of LVGL objects, because a live update deletes the old pages and fires SCREEN_LOADED again.

docs.title: Project id (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
• The app directory on the board was derived from the project name and board, so two projects named the same replaced each other. It now uses projectId, a UUID saved in the project. Save As to another path creates a new one; a file copied by hand keeps its id and still shares the directory.
  • Files without an id keep the name-based directory until the next save, so an unsaved reload does not create a new directory each time. Removing an autostart also accepts the old name-based path.
  • Old directories are not deleted: the IDE cannot know whether another project still uses them.

docs.title: Scaling to the chosen profile (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• Changing resolution, by picking a board, updating the profile or in the project settings, scales the project in one undoable step. Each axis scales on its own so the page stays full; shapes can stretch. Spacing props use the smaller factor, and fonts snap to the available sizes.
  • Scaling rewrites the saved values, so going to a small screen and back loses precision and font sizes. Undo restores them exactly.
  • The points of a Line widget are not scaled.

docs.title: LVGL sources in the packages (2026-11-07)
docs.text: • Packages include only src/, the top-level headers, LICENCE.txt and COPYRIGHTS.md of LVGL: this is what the C target compiles. Tests, demos, documentation and scripts added 150 MB and fonts that the IDE does not use.

docs.title: Visual tests (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• lvgl-mpy-studio test uses the same headless render as the designer preview, but runs the project code by default: the screen a user sees also depends on it. A Python traceback is an error even if a frame was drawn.
  • Baselines are PNG files, readable in any viewer and in Git, written by a small encoder in lvgl_mpy_studio/build/visual.py so the core does not import Qt. The reader accepts only that format.
  • Outside --update, a missing baseline fails, so a passing run always means a real comparison. --update renders twice and refuses unstable pages.
  • Version 1 captured each page once after loading. Scenarios with touch input came once the virtual clock made runs identical: see below.

docs.title: MCP server (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• lvgl-mpy-studio mcp is a separate stdio process with hand-written JSON-RPC, tested with the official Python client. The tool subset is small and the SDK would add many packages to the executables. The IDE gains only a menu switch, so the server costs nothing while it is unused.
  • By the owner's decision the agent has no limits compared to the IDE, board and autostart included, because a person supervises it. The only gate is the menu switch, off by default and read on every call. An unreadable setting counts as off.
  • simulate drives the runtime over the existing lvsim protocol, acting as a small headless IDE in lvgl_mpy_studio/sim/session.py. The runtime needs no change, and the app behaves as it does in the IDE panel. The clock was real at first; it is virtual by default since the next entry, and real only with clock: "real".
  • The server works on files, not on the open IDE, so version 1 has no shared undo and needs the project closed in the IDE.

docs.title: MicroPython export (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• The export writes the board files, not the simulator ones: the simulator display_driver.py talks to the IDE and cannot run on hardware. In the IDE, a project without a board asks for one, among those of the same resolution, and the choice is not saved in the project. The CLI and the MCP tool cannot ask, so they take a board id and otherwise refuse.
  • export_py/ holds .py sources and JSON metadata, no .mpy files. MicroPython imports a .py before a .mpy of the same name, so bytecode next to the sources would be ignored, and its format depends on a firmware the IDE may never have seen. Uploading from the IDE still precompiles.
  • Export overwrites its files, unlike the C export, because there is no handler stub to keep. The manifest stores their hashes, so the IDE asks before overwriting a file you changed, the CLI and the MCP tool refuse without an explicit flag, and all of them remove the files the project no longer needs.

docs.title: Single-file executable (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• For sending games on Linux, one file: a prebuilt launcher with the app appended as a ROMFS image, the format MicroPython mounts with vfs.VfsRom, followed by its size and a magic. The launcher is the same for every game, so building takes under a second and needs no compiler. Freezing the app into a new MicroPython build was tried first: it works, but needs the MicroPython sources and GCC on the user's computer, which the AppImage cannot ship.
  • The launcher reuses the Windows lvsim_standalone.c entry point and links a static SDL2 built from source with every backend loaded at runtime. The distribution libSDL2.a links about twenty libraries directly, libdecor among them, and a missing one would stop the game from starting.
  • The entry point sets sys.executable from /proc/self/exe, so a game started from PATH still finds itself, and limits sys.path to the app and .frozen: MicroPython always puts the current folder first, and a stray main.py next to the game would replace it.
  • License notices are frozen into the launcher and print with --licenses.
  • Self-extracting archives were rejected: they start slowly, write temporary files and, on Windows, often trigger antivirus warnings. Windows can follow with the same launcher design.

docs.title: Looking inside the simulated app (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• simulate can read and change the app state. The session adds a small module to its own copy of the project and calls it once per main loop iteration, after lv.timer_handler(). It reads JSON requests from standard input and answers on standard output with marked lines, which the session removes from the console. The runtime and the lvsim protocol do not change, and neither the board files nor the exports ever contain it.
  • Requests run between two frames, in the namespace of the module code, so lives or prepara_ondata() mean what they mean in the game. eval gets page() and objects() as extra names, without adding them to the module.
  • assert and wait_until stop the script at the first failure, so an agent reads one clear reason instead of a cascade.

docs.title: Simulated clock (2026-11-07)
docs.text:
• simulate uses a virtual clock by default. The session copy of the app replaces tick and wait in display_driver with a fixed 10 ms step and no sleep, and pauses after each loop iteration until the session asks for more time. Touch input goes through the same channel and lands at an exact simulated time, so a run is repeatable down to the pixel.
  • The game code sees the same time: sys.modules["time"] becomes a small clock that answers the ticks, the sleeps, time() and time_ns() with simulated time and passes the rest, such as localtime(), to the real module. The step is added in tick(), before lv.timer_handler(), so callbacks and LVGL see the same instant. seed calls random.seed.
  • No native change was needed: the time source and the touch state both live in the Python display_driver, and the session already uses its own copy.
  • The real clock stays available for a feel of the frame rate. The limit is 600 simulated seconds against 30 real ones, because the virtual run of a two-minute game takes a few seconds.

docs.title: Changing the resolution (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• A toolbar button changes the resolution in one click. Its menu lists the sizes of the known boards with their names, then common sizes, rotation and a custom size. The project settings dialog stays for the rarer cases. A board of another size is unlinked, with a note in the dialog.
  • Nothing moves on its own: every change asks for adapt, stretch or keep, and remembers the last answer. Keep stores designSize in each page, only while it differs from the display, so a page can be adapted later from the Arrange menu.
  • Adapt infers an anchor for each widget, like the Anchor property of Visual Basic, without asking for one. A widget that fills most of its container stretches with it; a small one near an edge stays at that edge; a large block or a widget in the middle keeps its centre in proportion. Sizes and fonts use one factor, so shapes keep their proportions, except on the axis where a widget stretches. Line points scale with their box in both modes. Two refinements came from rendering the examples: a widget drawn on a larger one follows it, as the dot on the Orbita ring, and close siblings move as one group, as the tic-tac-toe grid. Labels grow when their font is clamped to the smallest available size; buttons do not, or they would overlap.
  • An editable Anchor property can come later, if inferred anchors turn out not to be enough. The MCP keeps stretch as the default of set_resolution, so existing agent scripts do not change.

docs.title: Scenarios in visual tests (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• A scenario is a script of simulate steps with a name, a page and a seed, played on the virtual clock. Its screenshots and final screen are compared like pages. The step runner moved from the MCP server to lvgl_mpy_studio/sim/script.py, so the test command and the agent share it.
  • Scenarios live in scenarios.json next to the baselines of each resolution, because touch coordinates depend on it. The MCP save_scenario tool writes that file, so an agent can turn a tried simulate run into a test.
  • --update plays a scenario twice and refuses it if the two runs differ, as for pages. Simulated time starts on a fixed date, 1 January 2026, and localtime() follows it in UTC, so a clock on screen does not break a baseline, whatever the time zone of the computer. Steps are checked for shape before a scenario is saved or run.

docs.title: Portable single-file launcher (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• Built on Ubuntu 24.04 the launcher needed glibc 2.38, and dozens of its symbols come from 2.34 or later, starting with the threads that moved into libc. Pinning symbol versions was not practical, so runtime/build_onefile_portable.sh builds it in an Ubuntu 22.04 container. The result needs glibc 2.34.
  • The container builds its own mpy-cross in runtime/out/portable: the one in .reference belongs to the host and would not start inside. Intermediate paths are configurable for the same reason, so the container never mixes its objects with the host build. The final runtime/out/lvsim-onefile is replaced on purpose: the portable launcher also runs on the host.
  • runtime/build.sh still builds the launcher for the host, which is enough to develop. packaging/build.sh warns when the launcher would need a newer glibc, so a release does not ship it by mistake.

docs.title: Single-file executable for Windows (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• The Windows launcher reuses the Linux design: the same entry code and boot module, SDL2 linked statically from the MinGW development archive, ROMFS enabled with MICROPY_VFS_ROM, and -static so that only system DLLs remain. The IDE marks the copy as a GUI program before appending the app.
  • The launcher passes its own path in LVSIM_SELF, from GetModuleFileNameA on Windows and /proc/self/exe on Linux, so the boot module finds the appended app in the same way on both. The boot module falls back to sys.executable, so a launcher built before this change still works.
  • Bytecode does not depend on the system, so --for windows builds a Windows game on Linux and --for linux the other way round. The Windows build was verified under Wine: the frame matches the IDE render and a stray main.py next to the game does not replace it.

docs.title: Games in the browser (2026-11-08)
docs.text:
• The MicroPython WebAssembly port builds unchanged with our user C modules: the PyDevices LVGL 9.5 bindings, which were the main risk, compiled with Emscripten 7.0 at the first try, and lvsim draws through the Emscripten SDL2 on a canvas. Bytecode is the same format as on the desktop, so the game is the .mpy files the IDE already compiles, loaded into the in-memory file system.
  • The port already builds with ASYNCIFY. lvsim_sleep_ms calls emscripten_sleep, and the page starts the game with an asynchronous ccall, so the unchanged while display_driver.poll() loop gives the browser back control between frames. The default ASYNCIFY stack of 4 KB was too small for an LVGL game; it is 1 MB.
  • display_driver.py and the simulator buzzer tolerate the missing os.getenv. The buzzer prints its tone markers on WebAssembly too, and the page plays them with Web Audio after the first gesture, which browsers require.
  • The page needs an HTTP server because browsers do not load JavaScript modules from file://. The IDE serves the folder on 127.0.0.1 while it is open; lvgl-mpy-studio web does the same from the command line.
  • The runtime is about 6 MB and shared by every game. It is built by runtime/build_web.sh and not by runtime/build.sh, because it needs the Emscripten SDK, about 1 GB, which the CI does not install.

docs.title: Changes made outside the IDE (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• The MCP server and the CLI work on the project file, not on the open IDE. Before this, saving in the IDE silently replaced what an agent had written meanwhile. Now ProjectDocument keeps the SHA-256 of the bytes it last read or wrote. Project.save returns it and Project.load_with_revision computes it from the bytes it parses, so a save by the IDE itself is never taken for an external one.
  • Before writing the open file, save compares that revision with the file on disk. If they differ, it refuses with ExternalChangeError, and the window asks: reload the disk version, save a copy elsewhere, overwrite, or cancel. Cancel is the default; nothing is written without a choice. Overwriting means save(overwrite_external=True).
  • A deleted or moved file is a conflict too: saving would bring it back against the wishes of whoever removed it. The window then offers to recreate it or save a copy, with no reload. A file rewritten with the same bytes is not a conflict.
  • Save As, and therefore Save a copy, asks before replacing an existing file in the IDE itself, with QFileDialog.DontConfirmOverwrite, so the confirmation does not depend on the platform's native dialog. The copy is offered under a free name.
  • A reload clears the undo history, as opening a file does. A malformed file on disk fails the reload and leaves the document, its changes and its history untouched.
  • This is a check, not a transaction. A program that writes between the check and the atomic os.replace is still overwritten; the window is a few milliseconds. No lock files: they stay behind after a crash and behave differently on Windows. No file watcher yet: the IDE notices a change only when saving. A watcher and the expected_revision argument for MCP tools are the next steps in docs/architecture-evolution-v0.4.md.

docs.title: Project format for user modules (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• User modules are stored in the project file, under a top-level modules list of {id, name, source}. One file keeps undo, MCP, atomic saving and external-change detection working unchanged. core/modules.py module_files() is the only reader the pipelines will use, so separate .py files can come later behind it.
  • A project with modules is written as schemaVersion: 3; one without stays at version 2, byte for byte. This was tested on IDE 0.3.0, both the AppImage built on 2026-11-08 through its MCP server and the GUI from main (f0932d8):
  • version 2 with a modules key: 0.3 opens it, edits it, undoes and saves it, and keeps the key intact; but it generates no module file, so the app stops at start-up with ImportError: no module named 'utils';
  • version 3: 0.3 refuses it at once, in the GUI, the CLI and every MCP tool, with "Versione progetto non supportata: 3". A clear refusal is better than a project that opens and then fails at run time, and keeping version 2 for projects without modules means 0.3 users lose nothing they could open before. A requiredFeatures key would not have helped: 0.3 does not read it.
  • Module names are the import name and the file name: lowercase letters, digits and _, at most 31 characters, at the root of the app only. That rules out paths, .. and names that differ only by case, which collide on FAT, the file system of some boards (MicroPython documentation, not tested on our boards). The 31-character limit is a deliberate margin, not a measured file-system limit.
  • Refused names: files the IDE generates, anything starting with lvgl_mpy_studio, MicroPython modules with their u aliases, Python keywords and the names the IDE already reserves, __ names and handler names. On the simulator runtime, a time.py, json.py, random.py, asyncio.py or machine.py next to the app replaces the built-in module, while lvgl cannot be replaced (tested). A module named after a built-in would break the clock or the game.
  • Renaming or deleting a module never rewrites code. It returns the imports still using the old name, as renaming a widget does.

docs.title: User modules in every pipeline (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• generate_project writes the modules next to the generated files, verbatim except for line endings, so a traceback names the module's own file and line. It also writes a manifest.json with the file hashes and the ordered list of the app's Python modules. app_modules(directory) reads that list, and it is the only one: the single file (ROMFS), the frozen Release build, the Debug build and the web version all take their modules from it instead of keeping their own lists.
  • The manifest also tells what the previous generation wrote. A module that was removed or renamed is deleted with its .mpy, so stale code cannot hide an ImportError; files the generator did not write are never touched. Debug builds now drop old .mpy files as Release builds already did.
  • On the board, modules go into the package, the manifest and the bytecode precompilation, under the same all-or-nothing rule. A syntax error in a module names the module and its line instead of being mapped through the app_events.py source map. Stopping the app also forgets the modules loaded from the app folder.
  • Live editing treats a module change like any code change: a full upload. The designer preview ignores modules and the schema version, so neither editing a module nor going from version 2 to 3 redraws the canvas.
  • code_usage also scans the modules. import ui on its own line and from ui import a, b are understood; any other use of ui still exposes everything, the cautious choice. Projects without modules are analysed exactly as before.
  • The RAM budget runs the modules as bytecode, as on the board. The C export warns that Python modules are not part of it.
  • The simulator panel and the board console list traceback lines from modules with file and line, through build.compiler.traceback_errors, shared with the handler mapping.

docs.title: MCP tools for user modules, and file revisions (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• list_modules, create_module, rename_module and delete_module, plus module on get_code and patch_code as an alternative to handler, call core/modules.py and nothing else: names, reserved words, duplicates, references and patching live there once, shared with the future editor. The server only adds what MCP needs, an English "Unknown module" error listing the modules and the syntax check that set_handler and patch_code already did. A module must compile to be saved.
  • Existing tools keep their arguments, required lists and answers; new fields are only added. get_code without arguments still returns the shared code under module, now with modules and revision next to it.
  • project_info, get_code and list_modules return revision, the SHA-256 of the file bytes, as computed by Project.load_with_revision (identical to the code in the external-changes branch, so both branches agree on the value). Each tool that writes the project file accepts expected_revision and returns the revision it wrote, so an agent can chain changes without reading again.
  • A different revision is a revision_conflict error: isError, a JSON text and the same object in structuredContent, with expected_revision and current_revision (null for a deleted file). Nothing is written and nothing is retried: the agent reads again and decides.
  • The same check also runs without expected_revision, between the tool's own read and write, so a save by the IDE during a tool call is never overwritten. Agents that do not know about revisions only see an error in that race, which before was a silent loss.
  • It is not a transaction. Between the last check and os.replace another program can still write, and its change is lost; the window is the time of one atomic write. Without a lock, which we keep out for the reasons given for the IDE, it cannot be closed. Two MCP servers on the same file follow the same rule.
  • app_modules now stops with ManifestError when the manifest is missing, unreadable, without a module list, names something that is not a plain identifier, or lists a file that is not there. A broken manifest from an older run still never blocks the next generation, which rewrites it.
  • The MCP tests found that a version 3 file with widget events was read as if it were version 1, and failed to load: the check was version == 2. It is now version != 1, so version 3 reads events as version 2 does; the fix belongs with the version 3 format.

docs.title: Python modules in the editor (2026-11-10)
docs.text:
• The project tree ends with a Python Modules node, always shown so that a module can be created from its context menu: New, and on a module Open, Rename and Delete. Pages keep their positions in the tree. Modules are listed in project order, the order of the manifest, in the tree and in the code editor alike.
  • There is still one editor. A module is one more entry of the code panel's object list, Modulo: utils.py, next to the general code and the handlers, so highlighting, completion, typing merged into one undo step and syntax checking work as they do for the rest of the code. The panel follows a module by id, so it stays on it across a rename, an undo or a reload.
  • Every change goes through ProjectDocument.execute and the functions of core/modules.py: create, rename, delete and the text itself through set_module_source. The name dialog uses validate_module_name; an invalid name is explained and offered again for correction. Delete asks for confirmation and lists the code still importing the module; undo brings it back.
  • Rename and delete never rewrite imports. When code still imports the module, both ask first with a warning that lists it and names the risk, ImportError, with No as the default; afterwards the references also go to Output, with a status bar message. Renaming a widget or a page now also warns about modules that use the old name, still without rewriting them.
  • A syntax error in a module reads utils.py, riga 3: SyntaxError: invalid syntax and underlines the line; it never appears on the handler that imports the module. parse_compiler_errors now keeps the error line printed after the location as detail; handler messages are unchanged.
  • In a traceback, the last frame in user code is where the error happened (origin): the Errors panel lists it first, and the frames that led there, such as the handler that called the module, are marked "called from here". Activating a module row opens the module at its line.
  • The simulator prints tracebacks on stdout, not stderr, and a read can cut one in two. The window first parsed only stderr, so no row appeared and nothing could be clicked; the tests had fed the text in directly and missed it. Output is now buffered until a traceback is complete, whatever the stream, each row shows the exception and keeps the whole traceback as a tooltip, and the Errors panel comes to the front, since it sits behind Output.
  • An error in a handler does not stop the app, so the code stays read-only while the simulator runs, as before. That looked like a broken editor, and read-only text draws no cursor, so a row opened from the Errors panel seemed to land nowhere. While the simulator runs, a bar above the editor now says so, with a Stop and Edit button. The line of an opened error is highlighted, which shows in read-only text too, and stays until the code is edited.
  • What do you want to do? lists each module like a component: Import the module, its public functions with their arguments, classes and upper-case constants. They are read with ast, without running the module; with a syntax error the top-level def lines remain. Double-clicking inserts the call, with the cursor between the brackets when there are arguments. The open module shows its own group instead, expanded, as This module, with calls without the module prefix; leaving it out made a new module look as if the panel had not updated. While a module is edited, the list follows its functions after a short pause.
  • Generation never writes back into the project: a file edited by hand in the generated folder is replaced by the module's source at the next run.
  • A module is a file of its own, so ui and lv are not defined in it as they are in handlers, and the first user test stopped on NameError: name 'ui' isn't defined. A module created from the editor therefore starts with import lvgl as lv and import ui, the imports of the generated handlers, and a hint under the editor says so while a module is open. create_module in core/modules.py and over MCP still starts empty, so existing agents see no change.

docs.title: Browser demos
docs.text:
These applications and games run locally in your browser on one shared WebAssembly runtime. The flash and RAM figures are measured by the IDE; RAM is a 64-bit simulator estimate and overestimates 32-bit boards.

EIM-01

A five-page industrial monitor with live trends, alarms, diagnostics, and independent fan commands and telemetry.

TypeApplication Resolution1024 × 600 Flash98.5 KiB RAM253.1 KiB Play Source project Creation prompt

# EIM-01 — Ecosystem Industrial Monitor Use the lvgl-ide MCP server. **Specific version:** 0.1 **Application:** Embedded HMI for an experimental ventilation bench **Primary target:** 1024 × 600, STM32H743 **Secondary target:** 480 × 480, ESP32-S3 **Stack:** MicroPython + LVGL **Initial data source:** Internal simulation **Future data interfaces:** TCP/Wi-Fi, USB serial, BLE ## Objective Build an interactive HMI application to monitor and control a small ventilation bench with environmental and electrical sensors. The application must be editable visually in the IDE, runnable in the simulator, and deployable to compatible boards. All interface elements must be created through the GUI Builder MCP tools and remain editable in the original project. ## Screen 1 — Overview This is the main screen and must be usable on a 1024 × 600 touch display. **Top bar (56 px high)** - Logo/name: ECOSYSTEM | INDUSTRIAL MONITOR - Device identifier: EIM-01 - Communication status: ONLINE, OFFLINE, SIMULATION - Global alarm indicator - Settings button **Upper area with four numeric indicators** 1. TEMPERATURE: main value 24.6 °C, status NORMAL. 2. HUMIDITY: main value 48 %, status NORMAL. 3. FAN SPEED: speed 1450 RPM, target 1500 RPM. 4. POWER: power 7.4 W, supply 12.1 V. Each indicator must have a title, a large numeric value, a unit of measurement, and a small status indicator. **Central left area** A line chart of temperature over time, with a 60-second window and an update every second. It must also display a configurable alarm threshold, for example 40 °C. If the widget supports multiple series, humidity may be added on a separate scale; for the first version, a single quantity is preferable to ensure readability. **Central right area** A FAN CONTROL panel containing: - Requested speed: 0–100 %. - Touch-adjustable slider. - Actual speed in RPM. - AUTO/MANUAL mode. - START/STOP button. The panel must clearly show the difference between the requested command and the state actually confirmed by the system. **Bottom bar** - Status: SYSTEM NORMAL / WARNING / ALARM. - Last significant event. - Age indicator for the latest data. - Overview, Trends, Alarms, and Diagnostics navigation. ## Screen 2 — Trends Displays the trends of the monitored quantities. - Temperature chart. - Fan speed chart. - Selectable observation intervals: 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 15 minutes, where permitted by the available history. - Ability to pause chart scrolling without stopping acquisition. - Minimum, maximum, and average values over the selected interval. Data does not initially need to be saved permanently. A circular history in RAM is sufficient. ## Screen 3 — Alarms Displays and manages events and alarms. Initial alarms: - TEMP_HIGH: temperature above 40 °C. - FAN_STALL: speed well below the expected value for a configured interval. - SENSOR_LOST: invalid or unavailable sensor data. - LINK_LOST: interrupted communication. - POWER_LOW: voltage below the configured threshold. Each event must include a code, level, status, timestamp, and description. Distinguish at least the ACTIVE, ACKNOWLEDGED, and CLEARED states. The ACKNOWLEDGE button confirms that the alarm has been seen, but does not automatically remove the condition that produced it. ## Screen 4 — Diagnostics Displays technical system information. - Board name. - Firmware identifier. - Data protocol version. - Currently selected data source. - Connection status. - Received and discarded message counts. - Last received sequence. - Free memory, if available. - Uptime. - Any update times and LVGL performance metrics. Parameters unavailable on a particular target must be displayed as N/A, not as zero. ## Screen 5 — Settings - Data source selection: SIMULATION, TCP, SERIAL, BLE if available. - Alarm thresholds. - UI update frequency. - Connection settings. - Data simulator enablement. - Restoration of default settings. Do not issue physical commands or make persistent changes without a clear user action. ## Simulation mode Create a realistic, deterministic data generator that can be used without connected devices. The fan must respond to commands by changing RPM gradually, without instantaneous jumps. Temperature must evolve slowly, with a limited noise component. The application must support at least these reproducible scenarios: 1. Normal operation. 2. A progressive temperature increase up to the alarm threshold. 3. A fan that does not reach the requested speed. 4. A temporary loss of communication. 5. Recovery after a fault. The scenarios must be activatable in demo mode without changing the application code. ## Robustness requirements - Missing data must not cause an exception in the interface. - Numeric values must be validated before display. - A value that has not been updated must be marked as STALE. - A disconnection must leave the interface operational. - Charts must use fixed-size buffers. - The update cycle must not block the thread that manages LVGL. - Network and serial operations must have defined timeouts. - Settings must not be saved on every slider movement. ## MCP requirements The agent must create all screens and their widgets through the IDE MCP tools. Application logic must be separated from UI creation, maintaining a maintainable architecture. The generated application must be kept as an editable project and must be exportable to MicroPython. The agent must run tests in the simulator and document the results, without claiming that tests that were not run have passed. ## Acceptance criteria for the first version 1. All screens open without errors. 2. Overview displays data generated by the simulator. 3. The temperature chart updates in real time. 4. The slider changes the simulated fan setpoint. 5. RPM gradually reaches the expected speed. 6. A temperature fault generates an alarm. 7. The alarm can be acknowledged without clearing a condition that is still active. 8. Communication loss mode displays stale data. 9. The simulator continues to work after recovery. 10. The project remains editable in the IDE and exportable to MicroPython.
