docs.title: Install from the sources
docs.text:
On Linux you need Python 3.11 or later, a C compiler, CMake, pkg-config, SDL2 development headers, and xvfb for headless simulator windows. The first runtime build also downloads the pinned SDL2 sources.

git clone https://github.com/Copper-And-Code/lvgl-mpy-studio.git
cd lvgl-mpy-studio
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev]'
./runtime/build.sh
.venv/bin/lvgl-mpy-studio

The full requirements and the Windows and packaging instructions are in Building and testing on GitHub.

docs.title: Open a complete project
docs.text: Choose File → Open, select examples/eim-01/project.json, and press F5. The simulator runs the industrial monitor with the real LVGL runtime, including touch input and sound.

docs.title: Create your first project
docs.text:
1. Choose File → New.
  2. Drag a label and a button from the toolbox onto the page.
  3. Double-click the button and add its Python event handler.
  4. Press F5 to try the page in the simulator.
  5. Save the project as a single .json file.

The first-project walkthrough includes the handler for a tap counter. Continue with the user manual, the board guide, or Publishing on the web.

docs.title: How this project was built
docs.text: This page says who did what, so that a reader can judge the project for what it is.

docs.title: In short
docs.text: LVGL MPY Studio was designed and directed by one person, Nunzio Raciti, and written for the most part by AI coding agents working under his direction. It is not a hand-written code base with an assistant's help, and it is not an unattended output either: it is an experiment in how far one engineer can take a whole product by directing agents, and a statement of the method used to keep the result under control.

docs.title: Who did what
docs.text:
The author

  • chose what to build and in which order, and what to leave out;
  • set the constraints: the targets, the pinned versions of MicroPython and LVGL, the licences, English as the language of the code, what may be published and when;
  • decided between the alternatives the agents proposed, and rejected some;
  • owns the hardware: boards, firmware, wiring, and the judgement of what is seen on a display;
  • wrote the STM32H743 display and touch drivers himself, months before this project, and proposed them upstream; they were later ported to a repository of their own with the help of AI agents. The stack has the links.

The agents (Claude Code, with Anthropic's Claude models)

  • wrote most of the source code, the tests and the documentation;
  • reviewed the code in dedicated passes, and fixed what the reviews found;
  • ran the test suite, the simulator and, when asked, the boards attached to the author's computer;
  • reported what they had not verified. That list is in the status page.

Commits written this way carry a Co-Authored-By line naming the model. Nothing is hidden: of the 162 commits of the first two weeks, 139 carry that line.

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
• Decisions are written down with their date and reason, in decisions.md.
  • Every change comes with tests: more than 1250 automated tests, among them pixel comparisons between the MicroPython and the C output of the same project.
  • The IDE tests itself: lvgl-mpy-studio selftest drives the real window with mouse and keyboard through nine scenarios and reports each step. It found real defects that the unit tests had missed.
  • Each push is checked on other machines: the suite and the self-test run on Linux and on Windows in continuous integration.
  • Agents do not publish. Pushes, tags, releases and anything that touches a board need the author's explicit go-ahead.
  • Claims are separated from checks. A feature is described as tried on a board only when it was; everything else is marked as not verified.

docs.title: What this method does not give
docs.text:
• Human testing. The suite is large, but few people have used the IDE. Much that is written and tested by machine has never been tried by a person on a real task. This is the main weakness of the project and it is stated plainly in the status page.
  • Breadth before depth. Features were added early when they were expected to be useful, so that the design would not have to be reopened later. The price is that several are complete on paper and thin in experience.
  • A long history to read. See below.

docs.title: The history of the repository
docs.text:
The project has a predecessor by the same author: lvgl-mpy-builder, a web tool in TypeScript, public under the MIT licence since November 2025. The first MicroPython generator of this IDE is a port of the one in that project, verified at the time against its output file by file; the projects in reference/corpus and the list of widgets come from there.

Work on the IDE started on 2026-10-28 under the name LVGL IDE. In two weeks it went through versions 0.1 to 0.4, a change of name, a change of the package and command names, the move from Italian to English for code, comments and documents, and several experiments that were dropped. That history has 162 commits, 18 branches and 21 pull requests.

On 2026-11-11, with version 0.5.0, the repository was started again from the state of the sources at that moment, as a single first commit. The reason is tidiness, not concealment: the old history mixed two names, two languages and discarded attempts, and was a poor base for anyone joining the project.

What this means for a reader:

  • the history visible here begins at 0.5.0; what came before cannot be inspected commit by commit;
  • the changelog lists what each version changed, from the first one;
  • decisions.md keeps the dated decisions of the earlier period;
  • the author keeps the earlier history.

The single first commit is therefore two weeks of work, not one day's.

docs.title: LVGL MPY Studio manual
docs.text:
LVGL MPY Studio is a visual environment for building graphical interfaces with LVGL and MicroPython, in the style of Visual Basic: you draw pages by dragging controls, write a few lines of Python for their events and try everything in a simulator that uses the same LVGL as the board. When you are ready you upload the app to a board, build an executable to send to others, or export the code.

This manual describes version 0.4. For details on boards see the board guide, for AI agents the MCP server guide. The manual is also available in Italian.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Download LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-x86_64.AppImage, make it executable and start it:

chmod +x LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-x86_64.AppImage
./LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-x86_64.AppImage

Nothing else needs installing: Python, Qt, the simulator and the MicroPython compiler are inside the file.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Extract the whole folder LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-<version>-portable-win64.zip and open LVGL_MPY_STUDIO.exe. Python does not need installing. If the IDE does not start, LVGL_MPY_STUDIO_console.bat starts it with a console that shows the errors.

The executables are not signed: at the first start Windows SmartScreen may show a warning. Choose More info → Run anyway.

There is also an installer (LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-<version>-Setup-win64.exe) that installs to %LOCALAPPDATA% without administrator rights.

docs.title: Language and theme
docs.text: The IDE starts in English and is also available in Italian: Settings → Language. The theme follows the system, light or dark.

docs.title: 2. Your first project in five minutes
docs.text:
Let us build a page with a button that counts taps.

  1. File → New (Ctrl+N). The project starts with an empty page called main.
  2. From the Toolbox on the left drag a Label onto the page, then a Button. While dragging you see the control on the page, already aligned to the grid.
  3. Select the label: in the Properties panel on the right change text to Taps: 0. The label is named label1, the button button1.
  4. Double-click the button. The Code tab opens on the handler of its main event, button1_clicked, as in Visual Basic.
  5. Type:
global taps
taps += 1
ui.label1.set_text("Taps: %d" % taps)
  1. At the top of the Code tab choose (General) and type taps = 0: this is the module code, run once at start-up.
  2. Press F5. The Simulator tab opens: click the button and the number goes up.
  3. File → Save (Ctrl+S). The project is a single .json file.

If you do not remember how to change a text or read a value, look at the What do you want to do? box next to the editor: a double click inserts the right code. See section 8.

docs.title: 3. The window
docs.text:
Area What it holds Toolbar New, Open, Save, Undo, Redo, Grid, zoom, the resolution button (for example 480×480), the run target selector (Simulator or a board), Start and Stop Toolbox (top left) The widgets to drag onto the page, by category, with a search box Project (bottom left) The pages and, under each, its widgets and components, then the Python Modules. The right-click menu manages pages and modules Central area One tab per page, the Code tab and the Simulator tab Properties (right) The properties of the selected widget, By Category or in alphabetical order, and the Events tab Bottom panels Output (messages), Errors (a double click goes to the line of code), Components (Buzzer and Timer of the page) and Device Console (REPL of the board) Status bar Messages, the flash and RAM budget and, if a board is connected, its state with the Disconnect button

Panels can be moved and detached; View brings them back if you close them.

docs.title: 4. Pages
docs.text:
A project has one or more pages, like the forms of Visual Basic. You manage them from the Project menu or by right-clicking a page in the Project tree:

  • Add Page, Rename Page, Delete Page.
  • Set Initial Page: the one shown when the app starts.

In code each page has a constant: the page Game is ui.PAGE_GAME. To go to another page:

ui.load_page(ui.PAGE_GAME)

When you rename a page its handlers follow it; if the code still uses the old PAGE_… constant, the IDE tells you in the output.

Every page has the SCREEN_LOADED event, raised when the page appears: it is the right place to prepare the state, for example to reset a game. You find it in the Code tab by choosing the page as the object.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
Category Widgets Basic Button, Label, Panel Input Slider, Switch, Checkbox, Text Area, Dropdown, Roller, Spinbox, Keyboard Display Arc, Bar, LED, Spinner Data Chart, Scale, Table Media Image, Image Button Container Button Matrix, Calendar, Line, List, Message Box, Span Navigation Menu, Tab View, Tile View, Window

Each widget has a name that is unique in the project, for example button1, which you use in code as ui.button1. You change the name in the Properties panel; the handlers follow it, and if the code still uses the old name the IDE tells you where.

A widget can sit inside another, such as a Panel: drag it onto the container. Its coordinates become relative to the container. Deleting, copying or duplicating a container takes the widgets inside it too.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
To show a picture, drag an Image onto the page and, in Properties, press the … button next to src and choose a file. The picture becomes part of the project:

  • it is converted to PNG, and made smaller if it is larger than the screen;
  • it is stored inside the project file, so the project is still one file to copy or send;
  • it goes wherever the project goes: simulator, board, executables, browser version and C export.

The picture has a name, such as logo.png, shown in src: type the same name in another Image to show it again. One Undo takes back both the choice and the picture.

On a board a picture costs memory: its PNG bytes, plus about 4 bytes per pixel while it is on screen. A 100×100 icon needs about 40 kB; a full 480×480 background about 900 kB, more than many boards have free. The output lists the pictures that are heavy, and the image widgets whose picture is not in the project.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text:
Text is drawn with Montserrat, the font built into LVGL, in the sizes the target has (see Resolution and the board guide). To use another font, or a size the board lacks, add a font to the project: in Properties, press … next to font and choose a .ttf or .otf file. Then set fontSize to any size.

  • The font file is stored inside the project file. Type its name in the font of another widget to use it again.
  • When the code is generated the font is converted for each size in use, with the printable ASCII characters and the characters of the widgets that use it. Text set from code can use those characters; a character the font does not have is listed in the output.
  • The glyphs are the same LVGL's own converter would make. Kerning, the fine spacing between particular pairs of letters such as “AV”, is converted too.
  • On a board each converted size costs memory, roughly two and a half times its size: about 30 kB for ASCII at 24 pixels. On upload the IDE warns when the fonts would take more than half the free RAM of the board. The C export includes the fonts of the project and loads them from memory, which needs LV_USE_FS_MEMFS in lv_conf.h.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Components are not visible on the page: they appear in the Components panel at the bottom.

  • Buzzer: it sounds on the board and in the simulator, through the computer speaker.
  • ui.buzzer1.beep(880, 60) plays 880 Hz for 60 milliseconds.
  • ui.buzzer1.tone(440) plays until you call ui.buzzer1.off().
  • On a board the sound goes where the profile says: a pin, or a speaker. If the profile has no buzzer, the calls do nothing.
  • Timer: it raises its TICK event every period milliseconds.
  • Properties period and enabled (whether it starts on its own).
  • In code: ui.timer1.pause(), ui.timer1.resume(), ui.timer1.set_period(500).
  • It is the right way to do animations and games: a while loop in the code would block the interface.
  • Digital Output (under Hardware): a pin of the board driven on or off, for an LED or a relay.
  • Properties pin, active_low (the output is on when the pin is low) and initial (on at start).
  • In code: ui.digital_output1.on(), .off(), .toggle(), .set(True), .value().
  • In the simulator there is no pin: each change is written in the Output panel.
  • Digital Input (under Hardware): a pin that is read, for a push button or a switch.
  • Properties pin, pull (the internal resistor), active_low and debounce in milliseconds.
  • Events PRESSED, RELEASED and CHANGED; in the handler, e is the input itself: e.value().
  • In the simulator the input changes only when the code calls ui.digital_input1.simulate(True).

The pin is what MicroPython calls it on that board: a number, such as 25, or a name, such as PA5 on the STM32 boards. The IDE does not know which pins the display uses: choose one that is free.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
Buzzer, Digital Output and Digital Input are blocks: folders with a description (block.json) and MicroPython modules. Other people can write blocks, and you can add them:

  • Settings → Manage Blocks… lists the blocks, where each comes from, its author and licence, and which components of the open project use it.
  • Add from Folder… installs the block in a folder you downloaded; Remove deletes one you installed; Reload reads the blocks folder again; Open Blocks Folder shows it.
  • A project keeps a copy of the blocks it uses that are not shipped with the IDE, so it opens on a computer that lacks them. Install from Project installs such a block on this computer.
  • The simulator runs the code of a block on your computer, as it runs the code of a project: install blocks from people you trust.

docs/blocks.md explains how to write one, with examples/blocks/blinker as the example.

docs.title: 6. Drawing the page
docs.text:
• Adding: drag a widget from the Toolbox onto the page. The grid (View → Grid) aligns it.
  • Moving and resizing: drag the widget or its handles. For exact values use x, y, width and height in the Properties panel.
  • Selecting several: drag a rectangle on the empty page, or hold Ctrl while clicking.
  • Copying: Cut, Copy, Paste, Duplicate (Ctrl+D) and Delete, also from the right-click menu.
  • Arrange: with two or more widgets selected you can align them left, centre, right, top, middle or bottom, and distribute them horizontally or vertically.
  • Drawing order: Bring to Front (Ctrl+]) and Send to Back (Ctrl+[). Widgets drawn later cover the earlier ones.
  • Real LVGL Preview (View): the page is drawn by the real LVGL, with the fonts and styles you will see on the board, instead of the designer's approximation.
  • Zoom: Ctrl++ and Ctrl+−; Fit to Window with Ctrl+0.
  • Undo and Redo apply to every change, code included.

docs.title: 7. Resolution
docs.text:
The resolution is that of the screen you draw for, and it is the same in the simulator. After a change the page is fitted to the window again. You change it with one click from the button in the toolbar, for example 480×480:

  • Board: the resolutions of the known boards, with their names.
  • Common: 240×240, 480×480, 1024×600 and 1024×1024.
  • Rotate: swaps width and height.
  • Custom…: any width and height.

When the resolution changes, the IDE asks what to do with the widgets. Nothing moves on its own:

  • Adapt keeps proportions: circles and squares stay so. Each widget follows what it sits near: an edge, the centre, the widget it is drawn on, or the group it belongs to, such as a grid of buttons. Widgets that fill almost the whole width, such as a background, grow with the screen; labels grow if their font cannot get smaller. It works towards larger and smaller screens.
  • Stretch scales each axis on its own: the page stays full, but shapes are distorted.
  • Leave them where they are changes only the screen. Each page remembers the resolution it was drawn for, and later Arrange → Adapt Page to Resolution… adapts it, one page at a time.

The choice is remembered for the next time, and Ctrl+Z undoes everything at once. On a small, crowded page something may overlap: widgets that end up outside the screen are listed in the output.

If the project is tied to a board with another resolution, the board is unlinked and the project goes back to the simulator; the dialog tells you first.

Project → Project Settings… offers the same resolutions, plus the board profile.

Code can read the real resolution, which helps a game fit any screen:

width = lv.display_get_default().get_horizontal_resolution()
height = lv.display_get_default().get_vertical_resolution()

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
As in Visual Basic, each event of a widget has a handler: a Python function that runs when the event happens. In the Code tab:

  • on the left you choose the Object: a widget, a page, a component, or (General);
  • on the right the Procedure, that is the event: CLICKED, VALUE_CHANGED, PRESSED, RELEASED, LONG_PRESSED, SCREEN_LOADED, TICK and others.

When you choose an event that has no code yet, the IDE creates the handler. A double click on a widget in the designer opens its main event directly: CLICKED for a button, VALUE_CHANGED for a slider or a switch, TICK for a timer.

You write only the body of the handler: the IDE wraps it in def button1_clicked(e):. The parameter e is the LVGL event, if you need it.

docs.title: (General)
docs.text:
The code of (General) is the module: it runs once, at start-up, before the first page appears. Put shared variables, constants and your functions there. Inside a handler, changing a module variable needs global, as in any Python program:

# (General)
score = 0

def add(points):
    global score
    score += points
    ui.points.set_text(str(score))

docs.title: Python modules
docs.text:
When the code grows you can split it into modules: .py files of the project, which handlers, the (General) code and other modules use with import.

  1. In the Project panel, right-click Python Modules and choose New Python Module….
  2. Give it a name, for example game: lower-case letters, digits and _. You cannot use the names of MicroPython modules, such as time or json, nor those of the files the IDE creates, such as ui or main, nor the name of a handler. If the name is not valid, the IDE explains why and proposes it again.
  3. The module opens in the code editor, already with import lvgl as lv and import ui. A module is a file of its own: ui and lv do not arrive on their own as in handlers, and everything it uses must be imported.
# game.py
import lvgl as lv
import ui


def show(text):
    ui.label1.set_text(text)

Then, in a handler or in (General):

import game
game.show("Hello from the module")

A double click on a module in the tree opens it; a right click renames or deletes it. The IDE never rewrites import lines: if the code still imports the module, before renaming or deleting it the IDE warns that those imports will stop with ImportError and lists where they are. Undo (Ctrl+Z) puts everything back.

Modules go wherever the project goes: to the simulator, to the board as bytecode, into executables and into the browser version. The C export does not include them, and says so.

docs.title: Using widgets
docs.text:
Each widget is ui.<name>, and its methods are those of LVGL. Some examples:

ui.label1.set_text("Hello")                        # change the text of a label
ui.button1.get_child(0).set_text("OK")             # change the text of a button
value = ui.slider1.get_value()                     # read a slider
on = ui.switch1.has_state(lv.STATE.CHECKED)        # read a switch
ui.label1.add_flag(lv.obj.FLAG.HIDDEN)             # hide a widget
ui.label1.remove_flag(lv.obj.FLAG.HIDDEN)          # show it
ui.button1.add_state(lv.STATE.DISABLED)            # disable it

docs.title: What do you want to do?
docs.text:
You do not need to remember the LVGL API. Next to the editor the What do you want to do? box lists, for each widget, the most common actions: change the text, read the value, hide, disable, open this page, read the screen width and so on. Search for an object or an action in the box at the top and double-click: the right code is inserted in the editor, with the cursor on the value to change. Modules appear here too, like components: Import the module, its functions, classes and upper-case constants. In the open module the This module group lists its functions, to be called without the name in front.

In the editor, after ui. or ui.label1., Ctrl+Space shows suggestions.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Syntax errors appear in the Errors panel when you start the app, and under the editor while you type; an error while running appears with its exception, and hovering over the line shows the whole traceback. A double click goes to the right handler or module and line, which is highlighted, even if the error happened on the board.

If the error starts in a module, the first line is that of the module; the handler that called it follows, marked called from here.

docs.title: Printing
docs.text: File → Print Sources… (Ctrl+P) prints the source open in the editor, or all the sources of the project: the general code, the handlers written as the functions they become, and each module, each starting on a new page. Pages carry the project and source names, the date and the page count; lines are numbered and coloured as in the editor, and a long line wraps instead of being cut. Preview… shows the pages first. To get a PDF, choose to print to a file in the system print dialog.

docs.title: 9. The simulator
docs.text:
• F5 (Run → Start) starts the app in the Simulator tab, with the real LVGL and the real MicroPython.
  • Shift+F5 stops it, Run → Restart starts it again.
  • The mouse acts as a finger, the keyboard works and the Buzzer sounds from the computer speaker.
  • The print calls of your code appear in the Output panel.

While the simulator is running the project is read-only: a bar above the editor says so, and the Stop and Edit button stops the app. An error in a handler does not stop the app, so after an error the simulator is usually still running.

docs.title: 10. Working with a board
docs.text:
The board guide explains everything in detail; here is the essential path.

  1. Connect the board by USB. It needs a MicroPython firmware with LVGL and the display driver; the requirements of each board are in the guide.
  2. In the selector next to Start choose the board. The project resolution becomes that of the board, and the IDE asks how to adapt the widgets, as in section 7.
  3. Press F5: if there is only one serial port it is used, otherwise the IDE asks once. The app is uploaded and run; the board console appears in Device Console, where you can also type commands to the REPL.
  4. Shift+F5 stops the app. Disconnect in the status bar frees the port for other programs.

Other entries of the Device menu:

  • Live Editing: with the app running on the board, every change to the page appears on the board in under a second, without uploading everything again. Code changes need F5.
  • Upload Project copies the app without starting it; Upload and Run copies and starts it.
  • Device Information: firmware, LVGL version, memory, touch and compatibility with the profile.
  • Install Autostart…: the app starts on its own when the board powers up. Remove Autostart… restores the earlier launcher, saved by the IDE.
  • Manage Board Profiles…: profiles describe display, touch, buzzer and requirements of each board.

Each project has its own identifier, so on the board it goes to a separate folder and does not overwrite other apps, even with the same name.

In the run target selector, Use as default for new projects makes new projects start with that board and its resolution.

docs.title: 11. Memory: flash and RAM
docs.text:
In the status bar the IDE shows how much flash the compiled app takes and how much RAM it uses at start-up, updated as you work. With a board chosen, the values turn yellow or red as you get near its limits.

RAM is measured in the simulator, which is 64-bit: on 32-bit boards real use is lower.

docs.title: Folder executable
docs.text: Run → Build Executable… creates in dist/<project>-x86_64/ (or -win64 on Windows) a folder with the game, the runtime and the licences. On Linux it starts with run.sh, on Windows with the .exe.

docs.title: Single-file executable
docs.text:
Run → Build Single-File Executable… creates one file, about 5 MB, to send to whoever only needs to use the app: dist/<project> on Linux, dist/<project>.exe on Windows. It opens with a double click, with nothing to install.

  • On Linux it starts on Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora 35, Mint 21 and later.
  • On Windows it uses only system libraries. It has no console: messages and errors go to <project>.log, next to the game.
  • --licenses shows the licences of the included components, --selftest draws a frame without opening the window.
  • From the command line you can build the file for the other system: --for windows builds the .exe on Linux, --for linux builds the Linux file on Windows. On Windows the Linux file comes as <project>.tar.gz, because Windows has no execute permission: extract it and start it.

docs.title: Browser version
docs.text:
Run → Open in Browser builds the web version of the game in dist/<project>-web/ and opens it in the browser. It is the same app, with the real LVGL and the real MicroPython compiled to WebAssembly: you play with the mouse or a finger, and the Buzzer sounds from the browser after the first touch, because browsers do not let a page play sound before a gesture.

To share the game with a link, copy the whole folder to a host, for example Hostinger, GitHub Pages or Netlify: the guide Publishing games on the web explains the steps, also for several games together. The page does not work when opened directly as a file, with a double click on index.html: the browser wants a web address. That is why the IDE opens it through a small local server, active while the IDE stays open.

docs.title: MicroPython code for a board
docs.text: Project → Export MicroPython Code… writes to export_py/, next to the project, the files for the board of the project, to copy by hand or to integrate into another project. If the project has no board, the IDE asks which one to use. If you changed an exported file, the IDE asks before overwriting it.

docs.title: C code
docs.text: Project → Export C Code… writes to export_c/ the files ui.c, ui.h, ui_events.c and ui_events.h, which depend only on lvgl.h and work in any LVGL project in C. The handlers are empty functions with your Python as a comment: you write the C code in ui_events.c, and the IDE keeps it at later exports.

docs.title: 13. Visual tests
docs.text:
Visual tests check that pages stay the same while the project changes.

lvgl-mpy-studio test project.json --update   # the first time: writes the reference images
lvgl-mpy-studio test project.json            # afterwards: compares pixel by pixel

The reference images are in visual/<width>x<height>/ next to the project. If a page changes, the command fails and writes <page>.diff.png with the changed pixels in red.

To test touches too, add scenarios in visual/<width>x<height>/scenarios.json:

{"scenarios": [{"name": "launch", "page": "main", "seed": 3, "steps": [
  {"action": "tap", "x": 512, "y": 300},
  {"action": "wait", "ms": 1500},
  {"action": "screenshot", "label": "ball"},
  {"action": "assert", "expr": "lives == 3"}]}]}

A scenario runs on a simulated clock, so every run is identical, dates included. Each screenshot and the final screen become reference images; a false assert or a Python error fails the test. The steps available are the same as those of the simulate tool of AI agents, described in the MCP server guide.

docs.title: 14. Command line
docs.text:
The IDE also has a command line, lvgl-mpy-studio (with the AppImage: ./LVGL_MPY_STUDIO-x86_64.AppImage <command>). Messages are in English; --language it switches to Italian.

Command What it does lvgl-mpy-studio opens the IDE; the project is then opened from File → Open or File → Recent Files lvgl-mpy-studio run project.json starts the project in the simulator lvgl-mpy-studio generate project.json generates the code (--target micropython, c or board) lvgl-mpy-studio build project.json builds the executable in dist/ next to the project; --profile release --single-file for the single file, --for windows or --for linux for the other system, --web for the browser version lvgl-mpy-studio web project.json builds the browser version, serves it and opens it; Ctrl+C stops it lvgl-mpy-studio test project.json visual tests; --update, --page, --scenario, --threshold lvgl-mpy-studio device list lists the connected boards; info, upload, run, stop, reset, repl, autostart-install, autostart-remove act on a board with --port lvgl-mpy-studio mcp starts the server for AI agents lvgl-mpy-studio selftest the IDE uses itself and reports what works; see below lvgl-mpy-studio --version shows the version

docs.title: Self-test
docs.text:
lvgl-mpy-studio selftest opens the IDE and uses it as a person would: it creates a project, takes widgets from the toolbox, sets their properties in the panel, types a handler, saves, starts the simulator and touches the screen. Other scenarios cover pages, resolution, pictures and fonts, Python modules, the Timer and the Buzzer, and errors. Each step is checked and written as PASSED or FAILED; the last line is RESULT: PASSED or RESULT: FAILED, and the command ends with 0 or 1.

  • Without options the IDE stays hidden and the run takes a few seconds. --show shows it at work, slowed down; --slow 800 sets the pause after each action in milliseconds.
  • The report goes to lvgl-mpy-studio-selftest/<date-time>/ in the current folder, or to the folder given with --output: report.txt, report.json, the projects it saved under work/, and for each failed step a picture of the IDE and of the simulator.
  • --list shows the scenarios; naming one or more runs only those.
  • Your settings, recent files and board profiles are not touched. Do not use the mouse or the keyboard on the IDE's window while --show runs.

It checks that things work, not how they look, and it does not use boards.

docs.title: 15. AI agents
docs.text:
LVGL MPY Studio can be used by an AI agent, such as Claude or Kimi, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The agent creates projects, draws pages, writes the code, tries the game in the simulator by touching the screen, measures memory and, with you present, works on the board.

The server is off until you turn it on from Settings → MCP Server for AI Agents. The MCP server guide explains how to connect it to your agent and what it can do. Two practical rules:

  • if the project is also open in the IDE, the IDE notices the agent's changes when you save, and asks whether to reload the file, save a copy, overwrite or cancel: nothing is written without a choice. Changes made in the IDE do not reach the agent until you save;
  • before letting the agent use the board, disconnect it from the IDE.

The same check applies to any program that writes the project file, the command line included. If the file was deleted, the IDE offers to recreate it or to save it elsewhere. Save As asks before replacing another file.

docs.title: 16. Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Keys Action Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Shift+S New, Open, Save, Save As Ctrl+P Print Sources Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z Undo, Redo Ctrl+X, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Del Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete Ctrl+D Duplicate Ctrl+A Select all Ctrl+], Ctrl+[ Bring to Front, Send to Back Ctrl++, Ctrl+−, Ctrl+0 Zoom in, Zoom out, Fit to Window F5, Shift+F5 Start, Stop Ctrl+Space Suggestions in the editor Ctrl+Q Exit

docs.title: 17. Common problems
docs.text:
The simulator does not start or closes at once. Look at the Errors and Output panels: an error in the module code, or in a SCREEN_LOADED handler, stops the app at start-up. A double click on the error goes to the line.

The project cannot be changed. While the simulator or an app on the board is running the project is read-only: press Stop and Edit above the editor, or Shift+F5.

NameError: name 'ui' isn't defined in a module. A module does not get ui and lv as handlers do: add import ui and import lvgl as lv at the top.

ImportError after renaming or deleting a module. The code still imports the old name: update the import lines the IDE listed in Output, or undo with Ctrl+Z.

The board does not answer: could not enter raw repl. A program on the board does not stop with Ctrl+C. The IDE insists with more Ctrl+C, which is enough for shells that ask for two, like that of some ESP32-4848S040 firmware. If it is not enough, close other programs that use the port, press the reset button of the board and try again.

No sound from the Buzzer on the board. The board profile must name a pin or a speaker; the built-in profiles do so where the board has a buzzer. If in doubt look at Device → Manage Board Profiles….

The serial port is busy. Only one program at a time can use it: close other serial terminals, or disconnect the IDE if an AI agent or mpremote needs it.

I changed the resolution and something overlaps. Ctrl+Z undoes it, then try the other choice, or fix by hand the widgets the output lists as outside the screen.

The single-file executable does not start on an old Linux. It needs glibc 2.34 or later, that is Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 or newer. On Windows, if it does not start, look at <project>.log next to the file.

Windows says the app is not safe. The executables are not signed: More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: From a prompt to an app
docs.text: This is a complete session of an AI agent building an app with LVGL MPY Studio through the MCP server, starting from one sentence. It is recorded so that it can be replayed: the calls are in examples/weather/mcp-session.json and the result is examples/weather/project.json. A test replays the session at every run of the suite and checks that it still builds the same app.

docs.title: The prompt
docs.text: Build a weather station for the ESP32-4848S040: the current temperature of a city, a five-day forecast, a button to change city, and a settings page to switch between Celsius and Fahrenheit. Check that it works before you finish.

docs.title: What the agent did
docs.text:
24 tool calls, in four steps. The agent read about 18,000 characters of answers in total.

Step Calls What happened Look around list_boards, create_project, list_widget_types (names, then five types), project_info The board is 480×480 and its profile listed fonts 14, 16 and 24 when the session was recorded, so the large temperature is asked at 24. The profile now lists 32 and 40 too, read from a real board. Draw add_widgets (23 widgets in one call), add_page, add_widgets, render_page, validate Two pages. The five forecast cards are panels with two labels each, added with their parent in the same call. The agent looked at the rendering of the page. Write the code create_module, set_module_code, set_handler × 6 A forecast module with the data and the unit conversion, a refresh() function in the shared code, and one short handler per event. Check simulate, save_scenario, visual_test × 2, measure, project_info The simulator played taps on the buttons and the switch, with assertions on the texts. The same steps were saved as a scenario with reference images.

The app worked at the first run of simulate: 24 °C for Catania, Milan after a tap, 53 °F after switching units on the settings page, and the "updated N s ago" line counting on the simulated clock.

forecast.fetch() returns fixed data, so the app runs the same in the simulator and in the tests. On the board, with Wi-Fi, it is the one function to replace with a call to a weather service.

docs.title: What the session changed in the server
docs.text:
Playing the agent showed four places where it had to guess or pay more than needed. They are fixed, and the recorded session uses the fixed tools:

  • Answers were indented JSON. They are compact now: the whole session costs the agent about half the characters.
  • list_widget_types returned every type at once, 34,000 characters. It now takes names_only and types, and also returns the default values of each type.
  • list_boards did not say which font sizes a board has. It does now.
  • Text that cannot be drawn as asked was silent. A font size the board lacks, or a character outside the built-in font such as …, is now reported in the warnings of the call that sets it and by validate.

docs.title: Replaying it
docs.text:
QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen python -m pytest tests/test_mcp_demo.py

To open the result, load examples/weather/project.json in the IDE and press F5, or run:

lvgl-mpy-studio run examples/weather/project.json
lvgl-mpy-studio test examples/weather/project.json

docs.title: MCP server for AI agents
docs.text:
lvgl-mpy-studio mcp lets an AI agent work on LVGL MPY Studio projects through the Model Context Protocol, over stdio. The agent can create and edit projects, see pages rendered by the real LVGL runtime, run tests, build, and work on a connected board.

From a prompt to an app shows a complete recorded session: an agent builds a weather station in 24 calls.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
The server is off by default. Turn it on under Settings → MCP Server for AI Agents. While it is off, lvgl-mpy-studio mcp refuses to start, and a running server answers every tool call with an error. The choice is stored in lvgl-mpy-studio/mcp.json in your configuration folder.

This switch controls the MCP server only. It does not restrict the CLI.

docs.title: What the agent can do
docs.text:
There are no limits compared to the IDE. With the server on, an agent can run project code on your computer, upload and run code on a board, execute MicroPython on it and install autostart. Stay in control of the session, especially with projects you did not write: text inside a project can try to steer an agent.

Area Tools Project create_project, project_info, validate, set_resolution, adapt_page, list_boards, set_board Images and fonts add_image, remove_image, add_font, remove_font; project_info lists them Design list_widget_types, list_blocks, add_page, rename_page, remove_page, add_widget, add_widgets, update_widget, move_widget, remove_widget Code get_code, patch_code, set_handler, set_module_code, suggest_code Python modules list_modules, create_module, rename_module, delete_module Checks render_page, simulate, visual_test, save_scenario, measure Output generate_code, build Board device_list_ports, device_connect, device_disconnect, device_info, device_upload, device_stop, device_reset, device_exec, device_read_console, device_live_update, device_autostart_install, device_autostart_remove

list_widget_types returns every type with its properties, default values and events; the list is long, so names_only returns just the names and types the details of the ones asked for. list_blocks describes the blocks: non-visual components such as Digital Output and Digital Input, added with add_widget and used from code through their methods. list_boards gives the resolution and the Montserrat font sizes of each board. Text asked in a size the target lacks, or with a character outside the built-in font, is reported in the warnings of the call that sets it and by validate.

create_project takes width and height, or board for the resolution and board of a profile from list_boards; without them a project is 800×480. set_resolution takes mode: stretch, the default, adapt, which keeps proportions as in the IDE, or keep, which leaves the widgets alone so that adapt_page can adapt one page at a time.

Python modules are .py files of the project that handlers, the shared code and other modules import by name: import utils. create_module takes name and optional source; the name uses lower case letters, digits and _, and cannot be a MicroPython module such as time, a file the IDE generates such as ui, or a handler. get_code and patch_code take module instead of handler to read or change one. rename_module and delete_module never rewrite code: references lists the imports still using the old name. A module is a file of its own: ui and lv are not defined in it as in handlers, so its source imports them (import ui, import lvgl as lv). Unlike the editor, create_module does not add those lines.

project_info, get_code and list_modules return revision, a SHA-256 of the project file. Pass it as expected_revision to any tool that changes the project: if the file is no longer that revision, because the IDE or another agent saved it, nothing is written and the result is an error like this one, also in structuredContent:

{
  "error": "revision_conflict",
  "message": "The project file is not the revision expected: nothing was changed. Read it again with project_info or get_code, then repeat the change if it still applies.",
  "project": "/home/me/game/project.json",
  "expected_revision": "6f1c…",
  "current_revision": "a93e…"
}

Tools that change the project return the new revision, valid for the next call. Without expected_revision the tools work as before, and still refuse to write if the file changed while the tool was running. The check is not a lock: a program writing at the very moment of the save can still be overwritten.

render_page returns a PNG and runs the project code unless design_only is set.

simulate runs the app in the real simulator and plays a script of steps: tap, press, move, release, drag, key, wait, screenshot, repeat and reset_redraw. It answers with the console, any Python traceback, the buzzer tones, the frame count, whether the app is still running, redraw statistics, and one PNG per screenshot plus a final one. This lets an agent play a game or try a handler without a board. Each run starts the app from scratch.

By default the clock is virtual: the game advances in fixed 10 ms steps only while the script waits, and stops in between. A run is repeatable, screenshots included, and much faster than real time: a two-minute game takes a few seconds. time.ticks_ms(), ticks_us(), the sleeps, time(), time_ns(), localtime() and gmtime() follow the simulated time, which always starts on 1 January 2026 at midnight, with local time in UTC, so dates and times on screen repeat on every computer, and seed seeds random. A script can wait 600 simulated seconds at most. clock: "real" runs in real time like the IDE panel, up to 30 seconds, and gives a feel of the frame rate.

Four steps look inside the running app, between two frames, in the namespace of the module code:

  • eval reads an expression, such as lives or (score, wave), into values.
  • exec runs code to reach a state quickly, such as wave = 8 followed by the function that prepares a wave.
  • assert checks an expression, or {"page": "Fine"} for the active page. A false one stops the script and fills failure.
  • wait_until waits for an expression or a page, up to ms milliseconds, 5000 by default, and also counts towards the time limit.

Expressions can call page() for the name of the active page and objects() for the number of LVGL objects on it. passed is true when no step failed, every eval worked, no traceback was printed and the app is still running. A failed eval does not stop the script, so later steps still run. If the app stops answering, the script ends there. This code is added only to the copy of the project that runs in the simulator, never to the board or to exported files.

save_scenario stores a simulate script as a visual test scenario for the current resolution, and visual_test with update writes its baselines. From then on the same touches must give the same pixels.

The redraw statistics say how many pixels the app redraws per frame and per second. A step reset_redraw starts the count later, to skip the start-up frames. They show the relative cost of a design, not the frame rate of a board, because a board can redraw differently.

Points come from x and y, or from widget for the centre of a widget. widget uses the project coordinates, so it is wrong for widgets that the code moves at runtime, as the adaptive examples do. Use a screenshot and x, y for those.

docs.title: Client configuration
docs.text:
Most clients accept this form. Use the path of your installed lvgl-mpy-studio or AppImage:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lvgl-mpy-studio": {
      "command": "/path/to/lvgl-mpy-studio",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The server edits project files. If the same project is open in the IDE, the IDE notices the agent's changes when it saves and asks whether to reload, save a copy or overwrite; it does not watch the file, so it shows them only after a reload. The server itself refuses to write over a save it has not read, except in the brief race described above.
  • Only one program can hold a serial port: disconnect in the IDE before using the device_ tools.
  • Agent changes do not enter the IDE's undo history. Use Git to review or revert them.
  • With the virtual clock, code that measures real time, such as a benchmark, sees simulated time instead. The redraw statistics then describe simulated seconds: use clock: "real" for a feel of the frame rate on a PC, which still says nothing precise about a board.
  • Long board operations block the server until they finish, and some clients stop waiting after a timeout.

docs.title: Publishing games on the web
docs.text:
Italiano

This guide explains how to put online one or more games made with LVGL MPY Studio, so that anyone can play them in the browser from a link, also on a phone. The example uses Hostinger, but the steps apply to any web host: it is only a matter of copying files.

No special server or database is needed: the web version of a game is a folder of static files.

docs.title: 1. Building the web version
docs.text:
For each game:

  1. Open the project in the IDE.
  2. Choose Run → Open in Browser. The IDE creates the folder dist/<game>-web/ next to the project and opens it in the browser: try it there before publishing.

Or, from a terminal:

lvgl-mpy-studio build project.json --web

The folder holds:

File What it is for index.html the page of the game lms_web.js starts the game and plays the Buzzer micropython.mjs, micropython.wasm MicroPython and LVGL compiled for the browser, about 6 MB, the same for every game game/ the compiled game licenses/ the licence notices of the included components .htaccess tells the server what kind of files .wasm and .mjs are

The .htaccess file starts with a dot, so many programs hide it: it is there, and it is needed. See section 5.

Build the folder again every time you change the game: the IDE replaces it.

docs.title: 2. Organising one or more games
docs.text:
Each game goes in its own folder. For simple addresses, rename it in lower case and without spaces. A convenient layout:

public_html/
└── games/
    ├── index.html         ← list of games, optional (section 4)
    ├── breakout/          ← the content of dist/Breakout-web/
    │   ├── index.html
    │   ├── .htaccess
    │   └── …
    └── orbit/             ← the content of dist/Orbit-web/
        ├── index.html
        └── …

The addresses become https://yourdomain.com/games/breakout/ and https://yourdomain.com/games/orbit/.

Each folder holds a copy of the 6 MB runtime. With a few games this is not a problem, and the browser downloads the runtime only once per game.

docs.title: With the File Manager, the simplest way
docs.text:
1. On your computer, compress each folder into a ZIP. On Linux, from the dist folder:
cd dist
cp -r Breakout-web breakout && zip -r breakout.zip breakout && rm -r breakout

On Windows: right-click the folder → Compress to ZIP file, after renaming it to breakout. The ZIP keeps the .htaccess file too. 2. Go to hPanel, open the site and go to Files → File Manager. 3. Enter public_html and create the folder games: public_html is the folder of your site, and what is in it shows at https://yourdomain.com/. 4. Enter games, upload breakout.zip with the upload button, then right-click the file → Extract. The folder breakout must appear with index.html inside. 5. Delete the ZIP. 6. Repeat for the other games.

docs.title: With FTP, convenient if you update often
docs.text:
1. In hPanel → Files → FTP Accounts you find server, user and password, and can create one.
  2. Connect with an FTP program, for example FileZilla, using those details.
  3. Drag the game folders into public_html/games/.
  4. In FileZilla, to see and upload .htaccess too, turn on Server → Force showing hidden files.

docs.title: Trying it
docs.text: Open https://yourdomain.com/games/breakout/ in the browser. "Loading…" appears, then the game. The first time loading takes a few seconds, to download the runtime; afterwards the browser keeps it in its cache. Sound starts after the first touch or click on the page, because browsers do not let a page play sound before a gesture.

docs.title: 4. A page listing the games
docs.text:
Optional, but convenient to share: one link for all the games. Save this file as index.html inside public_html/games/ and adapt the list:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>My games</title>
<style>
  body { margin: 0; padding: 24px; background: #101318; color: #d8dde6; font: 16px system-ui, sans-serif; }
  h1 { font-weight: 600; }
  ul { list-style: none; padding: 0; display: grid; gap: 12px; max-width: 480px; }
  a { display: block; padding: 16px 20px; border-radius: 10px; background: #1d2430; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; }
  a:hover { background: #2a3445; }
  small { display: block; color: #9aa4b2; margin-top: 4px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
<h1>My games</h1>
<ul>
  <li><a href="breakout/">Breakout<small>Drag the paddle, break the bricks</small></a></li>
  <li><a href="orbit/">Orbit<small>Defend the ring from the swarm</small></a></li>
</ul>
</body>
</html>

Each entry points to the folder of the game, with the trailing slash.

docs.title: 5. If the game does not start
docs.text:
Open the developer tools of the browser (F12), Console tab.

"Failed to load module script… MIME type" or "Incorrect response MIME type. Expected 'application/wasm'" The server does not know what kind of files .mjs and .wasm are. Check that .htaccess is in the folder of the game. If you do not see it in the File Manager, look in its settings for the option to show hidden files. If it is really missing, upload it again, or create it with this content:

<IfModule mod_mime.c>
    AddType application/wasm .wasm
    AddType text/javascript .js .mjs
    AddType application/octet-stream .mpy
</IfModule>
<IfModule mod_deflate.c>
    AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE application/wasm text/javascript application/json
</IfModule>

You can check the result in the Network tab: clicking micropython.wasm, the Content-Type header must be application/wasm. If .htaccess is there but nothing changes, ask Hostinger support to enable those MIME types for the site.

"404" on game/files.json or on a .mpy file The game folder was not uploaded, or ended up in the wrong place. It must be next to index.html.

The page stays blank or on "Loading…" when opened as a file You opened index.html with a double click from your computer. The browser wants a web address: use the address of the site, or Run → Open in Browser from the IDE.

The game works but there is no sound Touch or click the page once: sound starts only after a gesture. Also check that the browser tab is not muted.

The game is slow on an old phone MicroPython and LVGL run in the browser, so on a weak phone a game with many moving objects can slow down. The Memory section of the manual and the redraw statistics of simulate help to see how much work the game does at each frame.

docs.title: 6. Other hosts
docs.text:
The same steps apply elsewhere:

  • Other hosts with Apache or LiteSpeed, such as SiteGround or OVH: copy the folders with the File Manager or FTP. The included .htaccess should work; if the game does not start, check the MIME types as in section 5.
  • GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages: they already know .wasm and .mjs, and the .htaccess file is ignored. Just upload the folders, or drag them onto the Netlify upload page.
  • Nginx on your own server: .htaccess does not count. Check that /etc/nginx/mime.types holds application/wasm wasm; and text/javascript js mjs;.

docs.title: The stack, from the display controller to the agent
docs.text:
LVGL MPY Studio is the top of a stack that goes down to the registers of the display controller. This page follows one frame from the silicon to the tool an AI agent calls, and says in which repository each layer lives.

Layer What it does Where 7. Agents An AI agent designs, runs and tests an application through 49 tools this repository, mcp_server.py 6. IDE Designer, code editor, generators, board upload this repository 5. Simulator The same MicroPython and LVGL on the PC, and in the browser as WebAssembly this repository, native/lvsim, runtime/ 4. Contract What an application may assume of a board: display_driver, the board profile both repositories 3. Binding import lvgl as lv in MicroPython, generated from LVGL's headers omnipython-lvgl, by PyDevices, pinned and unchanged 2. Firmware MicroPython boards built out of tree, with frozen drivers mpy-lvgl-boards 1. Display drivers C modules that put pixels on an RGB panel mpy-lvgl-boards, modules/

docs.title: Layers 1 and 2: registers and firmware
docs.text:
The firmware is a separate repository, mpy-lvgl-boards, by the same author. Its documents hold the measurements and the bench logs; what follows is a summary of what is there.

  • STM32H743, modules/st_ltdc. The LTDC and the DMA2D are programmed through their registers, without the HAL sources for those peripherals. Frame buffers live in a region of the SDRAM that is never freed, because the LTDC keeps reading it across a soft reset. Partial updates are copied into the shown buffer by the DMA2D. Frames and underruns are counted and can be read from Python.
  • RP2350, modules/rgbpanel. The RGB panel is scanned out by a PIO program fed by DMA. The DMA block that ends a frame reads the list for the next one, in hardware, so no interrupt runs per frame.
  • ESP32-S3, modules/esp_rgb. The RGB panel of the ESP32-4848S040 through ESP-IDF.
  • Boards out of tree. No fork of MicroPython or of the binding: board definitions, user C modules and a patches/ folder applied by the build script, on pinned sources.
  • Tests on the board. tests/hil/ runs on the hardware with mpremote: panel, touch, performance, a soak test, behaviour when LVGL runs out of memory.

The frame rates, the soak times and the state of each board are in that repository's README and are not repeated here, so that they have one source.

docs.title: Where the STM32H743 drivers come from
docs.text:
They are older than this project. The author wrote the LTDC display driver, the GT911 touch driver and the board definitions himself and proposed them upstream in March 2026:

  • lvgl/lv_binding_micropython #407, the LTDC display and GT911 touch drivers: about 2900 lines in 14 files, with the C module, the board support for three boards and the Python layer that selects board and panel;
  • lvgl/lv_micropython #104 and #105, the STM32H743 board family.

Those pull requests are still open; the first has had no review from a maintainer. In May 2026 the author paused them, saying so in the pull request, and took the same work to the lvgl_micropython project, asking its maintainer which architecture a contribution should follow: discussion #577, which ran until August with 8 threads and 45 replies. That repository has had no commits since June 2026, and the series was not submitted there.

In November 2026 the code was ported, with the help of AI agents, to a repository of its own on top of omnipython-lvgl, a binding under active development. One change needed there went upstream and was merged: PyDevices/omnipython-lvgl #6, LVGL memory pools on ports without multi_heap.

docs.title: Layer 4: the contract
docs.text:
The IDE does not know a board's pins. It relies on two things the firmware provides:

  • a frozen module, display_driver, with start(), stop(), WIDTH, HEIGHT, BUFFERS and indev; import display_driver is all a generated application needs;
  • facts read from the running board on connection: MicroPython and LVGL versions, the bytecode version, the built-in font sizes, whether fonts can be loaded at run time, free RAM and free space.

A board profile, a JSON file in lvgl_mpy_studio/boards/, holds what cannot be read: the name, the resolution, the adapter, the serial protocol. When the board and the profile disagree, for example on the font sizes, the board wins and the IDE says so.

docs.title: Layers 5 and 6: this repository
docs.text:
Places worth reading first:

File Why lvgl_mpy_studio/device/uart.py A raw-REPL transport written for the STM32H7 boards, reached through a UART adapter: chunked writes that stay inside the raw REPL lvgl_mpy_studio/device/service.py Upload as a transaction: staging folder, size check, rename, rollback lvgl_mpy_studio/gen/binfont.py, fontconv.py A TrueType to LVGL binary font converter, kerning included, compared in the tests with LVGL's own Montserrat native/lvsim/ The C side of the simulator and its protocol, shared by the MicroPython and the C targets lvgl_mpy_studio/gen/ The generators: one project, MicroPython and C, compared pixel by pixel in the tests lvgl_mpy_studio/core/blocks.py Blocks: hardware components described by data, read without ever running their code lvgl_mpy_studio/selftest/ The IDE driving itself with mouse and keyboard

docs.title: Layer 7: agents
docs.text:
The MCP server exposes the same operations as the IDE: create a project, add and change widgets, write handlers and modules, render a page with the real LVGL, play touch input on a simulated clock, upload to a board and read its console. From a prompt to an app is a recorded session of 24 tool calls, replayed by a test.

The case study, an industrial monitor of 5 pages and 256 widgets, was built this way from a prompt.

Two details matter more than the number of tools:

  • Revisions. Every tool that changes a project can be given the revision the agent last read; a file changed in the meantime is reported as a conflict and left untouched. The IDE applies the same check when saving. An agent and a person can work on one file.
  • The same renderer. What an agent sees from render_page is the frame the board draws, produced by the same MicroPython and LVGL, not a mock-up.

docs.title: What this stack does not show yet
docs.text: A complete device going through all seven layers. The case study stops at layer 5: its data are simulated. The blocks for I2C and PWM, which would let it read a real sensor and drive a real fan, are planned and not written.

docs.title: Status: what is verified, and how
docs.text: Version 0.6.0 is tagged in the repository. No release with packages has been published. This page separates what has been checked from what has only been written.

docs.title: Read this first
docs.text: The project was built broad on purpose: features expected to be useful were included from the start, so that the design would not need to be reopened later. The automated tests are many. Human testing is scarce: few people have used the IDE, and much of what is listed below has never been tried by a person on a real task. Expect rough edges, and treat every "not tried" below as an open question, not as a formality.

docs.title: How each area was checked
docs.text:
• Tests: covered by the automated suite, more than 1250 tests.
  • Self-test: exercised in the real IDE window by lvgl-mpy-studio selftest.
  • Board: tried on real hardware, with the board named.
  • Not tried: written and tested by machine only, or not at all.

fonts in C on a board Upload progress window yes RP2350: the figures it shows the window itself, watched by a person Buzzer yes yes, in the simulator on a board Block: Digital Output yes, with a fake machine yes, in the simulator STM32H7_CORE: the two LEDs of the board on pins B0 and B1, driven from a Timer, the pin levels read back and the LEDs seen by the author other boards Block: Digital Input yes, with a fake machine yes, in the simulator STM32H7_CORE: the two keys of the board on pins A0 and A1; the author saw the LEDs follow the keys other boards; the debounce, which was not measured Block Manager, blocks from other people yes used by a person; a block written by someone else Browser version (WebAssembly) yes Chromium, two resolutions Firefox, Safari, phones Single-file executables yes, on Linux and under Wine Linux Windows, natively Windows yes, under Wine, and natively in continuous integration yes, on Windows 11 from the portable package and in continuous integration the portable package of 0.6.0 started by the author on Windows 11 boards and builds on Windows MCP server yes, and a recorded session the board tools, on hardware Visual tests yes used on the EIM-01 example Print Sources yes a PDF, read a real printer Self-test, visible mode (--show) never run AppImage for Linux yes, run from inside the package built from the sources of 0.6.0 on the author's computer: self-test, visual tests of EIM-01, board and C generation, single-file games for Linux (needing glibc 2.34 or later) and Windows, browser version on another Linux system Portable Windows package built for 0.6.0; its contents inspected: no bundled ICU, the icon in the program file, the blocks; started by the author on a real Windows the installer, never built

"Author's use" means the author uses it while developing; it is not a test plan.

docs.title: Known defects and open points
docs.text:
• Windows. The portable package of 0.4 did not start on a real Windows: it bundled a copy of ICU that hid the system's. The package of 0.6.0 is built without it and starts on Windows 11. The self-test run there passed 76 steps of 78. The step that failed was a mistake of the self-test, which compared a path written with \ with the same path written with /; the step after it was skipped. The run also showed a real defect: when the program ended while a measurement was running, a simulator process stayed alive and its temporary folder could not be removed. Both are corrected, and the author ran the corrected package on Windows 11 without that error. Tests under Wine had shown neither. A third defect, reported by the author, is corrected and not yet seen on Windows: started from the program file, a console window flashed four times at almost every operation.
  • The IDE does not know the pins of a board. A block takes the pin the user types, a number or a name such as PA5, and nothing warns when it is one the display or the memory already uses.
  • The RAM budget shown in the status bar is measured in the 64-bit simulator and is an overestimate for 32-bit boards.
  • Renaming a Python module does not rewrite the code that imports it; the IDE warns.
  • Reference images that hold a changing value fail when the generator changes: the EIM-01 example shows the free memory on a page, and its image had to be regenerated for 0.6.
  • Continuous integration covers tests, not packages. Since the repository became public, each push runs the whole suite and the self-test on Linux, and on Windows the tests of the core, of the runtime and of the IDE, and the self-test. On the Linux machine 72 tests are skipped, because they need what is not built there: the launchers of single-file games, the WebAssembly runtime, Wine, a browser. Packages are built and checked by hand.
  • An upload sends every file again, also those that did not change: a project with fonts takes tens of seconds on a slow link each time.

docs.title: What is not there
docs.text:
• The pages that Help → Online Documentation opens: they will be published when the repository becomes public; until then the link leads nowhere.
  • C on boards: only MicroPython is uploaded. The C export is source code for another project.
  • An online catalogue of blocks, and blocks that depend on other blocks.
  • Extensions that run inside the IDE: blocks are data and MicroPython code, nothing more.
  • Blocks for PWM, ADC, I2C, SPI and UART: planned in the plan, not written.
  • A debugger. Errors are reported with file and line; there are no breakpoints.
  • macOS.

docs.title: How to check for yourself
docs.text:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q        # the whole suite, about ten minutes
.venv/bin/lvgl-mpy-studio selftest   # the IDE uses itself, about twenty seconds

The self-test writes report.txt with one line for each step. A step that fails is a defect worth reporting.
